logline: Six people, one minivan and nineteen hundred miles of Interstate 10; a phone call at a gas station in Arizona; a long dark in West Texas; and a house on Dupre Street that has been told who’s coming.

s01.slug: FRIDAY · 8:05 AM · I-405 SOUTH, THE SEPULVEDA PASS
body: The 405 climbs the Sepulveda Pass under a gray that has no intention of burning off, ten lanes of brake lights strung up the grade, and on its ridge above the southbound side the Getty sits white and square in the overcast like a hospital for paintings. The Odyssey is doing eleven miles an hour. Kevin is doing it at exactly the speed of everyone around him, both hands on the wheel, the La Vang rosary hanging dead still under the mirror, because nothing in Los Angeles is moving fast enough to swing it.

The second of the two Carpenters songs on Kevin’s *Road Trip Mix* comes up out of the door speakers at the volume his mother left the knob on, and it plays to the end with six people listening to it and not one of them remarking.

body.text: Theo is asleep in the passenger seat in MEDIUM SPARKLE’s satin mask again, chin down in the collar of his camel coat, his mouth a little open, a silent-film heiress on the second reel.
body.else: Theo is asleep in the passenger seat with his own hand over his eyes again, his head against the glass and his camel coat buttoned to the throat against a morning he has declined to attend.

body: Across the aisle Margot has Interstate 10 on her knees, printed out county by county and laid over Gloria’s box, the top sheet already gone three colors.

body: Her tape recorder rides in the milk crate between her Docs with its red light off. When Jack’s eyes go to it, she doesn’t move anything but her mouth. “I don’t record captivity,” she says. “There are ethics boards.” Between Jack’s boots FIREMAN, LARGE sits on the floor mat with its grosgrain bows flopped over and the horseshoe pillow still sealed inside.

The rule from the packing still holds. It was never voted on, and it hasn’t been lifted: Lena doesn’t speak to Jack, Jack doesn’t speak to Lena, and anything that has to cross the van crosses it by way of Kevin or Laney. In a parking lot it was a procedure. In a minivan on the 405, with six people sitting close enough to hear each other swallow, it is a play with the house lights up.
From the way-back, behind Margot, diagonally as far from him as Kevin’s chart allows: “Kevin, it’s seventy-eight back here.”
Kevin, to the dash: “It’s seventy-eight back there.”
The rear climate dial is in the ceiling over Jack’s head. He reaches up and turns it down two clicks and says, to the back of Kevin’s head, “Down.”

“It’s down,” Kevin says, and moves them up four car lengths, the most progress anybody has made since Sherman Oaks. Under the Mulholland bridge a silver Prius noses into the gap ahead of them, and Kevin, who has read about the brakes, lets it have three more lengths and the benefit of his prayers.
Up front Kevin glances at the dash clock and at the trip odometer, which he zeroed at the Chevron by the freeway, and does a sum he doesn’t share. Then he shares it. “Two hours. Ninety-one miles.”
“Theo said thirty hours,” Laney says from the way-back, her sunglasses still on.
“Theo is asleep,” says Kevin.
Margot uncaps a yellow highlighter and draws a very short line on Los Angeles County. “At this rate,” she says, “we make New Orleans for Lent.”

It’s a temperature. Jack can handle a temperature. At this size it suits him: a number out of the way-back, a dial in the ceiling, a word to Kevin, and the back of his own head toward her for nineteen hundred miles.

Past Wilshire Kevin signals for the 10 half a mile early and takes it east, and downtown stands up ahead of them in the overcast, glass and more glass, the tops of the tallest towers gone into the cloud. North of everything the San Gabriels have weather piled on them, slate-dark and heaped to the ridgelines, and it sits there over the foothills and doesn’t move.

Jack cracked his window at the Rincon for the cold and the salt, and it is still cracked, and now what it lets in is the 10: tire hum, a motorcycle splitting the lanes, somebody’s bass three cars over, the whole city breathing exhaust at a crawl. He hasn’t slept since Wednesday night. His eyes feel sanded. Somewhere north of all this the six-forty out of Goleta is over Oregon by now, with a girl in a window seat in it who is mostly fine about it, and the thought of her up there in the bright above the cloud deck, with her knees up and her coat for a blanket, is the one warm thing he has brought into this van.

choices.text: *Roll it up.*
response: He rolls it up. The glass seals, the 10 drops to a hum, and the van warms by a degree. Kevin’s mix moves on to something with a pedal steel in it. Jack puts his temple against the window with the RAZR shut in his fist and the book a hard rectangle in his back pocket, and somewhere past the East L.A. interchange he stops keeping track of the exits, and by El Monte he’s gone.

choices.text: “Kevin, tell her it’s a sunroof.”
response: “Kevin,” he says. “Tell her it’s a sunroof.”
Laney gets there before Kevin can, without lifting her sunglasses, in a voice like a frost advisory for the higher elevations: “He says it’s a sunroof.”
From the way-back: “Laney. Tell him it’s a *window*.”
“It’s a window,” Laney says, and turns her face back to the glass.

He runs it up halfway, as a statement, and leaves the rest open, as another. Kevin gains them three car lengths and gives them back. Jack props his head on the cold edge of the frame with the air coming across his eyelids, and is asleep by El Monte.

choices.text: *Leave it open and let Los Angeles in.*
response: He leaves it. Los Angeles comes in at the crack: diesel off a city bus in the next lane, the flat wet-concrete smell of the river channel as they cross it, carnitas from a taco truck parked at the foot of an off-ramp with its awning up and a line already at it.
From the way-back: “Kevin, I’m going to die of Los Angeles.”
“I’ll put it on the chart,” Kevin says.

Jack lays his head against the cold of the window frame, where the air comes in on his cheek and his ear, and somewhere around the Long Beach Freeway he loses the thread of the road, and by El Monte he’s asleep.

s02.slug: FRIDAY · 9:40 AM · I-10 EAST, ONTARIO → REDLANDS — TWO TRUTHS AND A LIE
body: Jack comes up out of most of an hour of sleep with the window printed down one cheek, because Theo is awake, and when Theo is awake the van is.

Theo is awake all at once, sitting up, taking in the Inland Empire through the windshield: a warehouse, a warehouse, a billboard for a personal-injury lawyer with his arms folded, a warehouse the length of an airport, the sky over all of it the same flat gray it was in Los Angeles, only with more room. He has his iPod out of his coat and the little transmitter plugged into the lighter socket, thumbing down the dial for a frequency San Bernardino County isn’t using, and he finds one, and the Carpenters give way to marimba and strings and four boys out of Columbia. Kevin lets it have most of a verse before he reaches across and presses the button for his CD.
“It’s my mother’s car,” Kevin says.

Theo puts the iPod back in his coat and turns around in his seat to face the van, awake now in every part of him. “Two truths and a lie,” he says. “To pass the Inland Empire. It’s that or the Inland Empire.”
Margot, referee by temperament: “I’ll allow it.”
“Rules,” Theo says. “Three statements. One lie. The lie has to be possible.” He looks into the way-back. “Laney.”
“*Possible* is a strong word,” Laney says. “For a Friday.”

He points at the driver. Kevin doesn’t take his eyes off the road. “One. Your stomach grows a new lining every few days, or it would digest itself. Two. You can’t tickle yourself; the brain cancels it out before it gets there. Three. I have had zero cavities in my life.”
“Kevin,” Theo says. “One of them has to be a lie.”
“Respectfully, I don’t lie.”
“Then it isn’t a game,” Theo says.
“It’s a game,” Kevin says. “I win it.”

Laney goes next, from the way-back, without being asked. “Okay. One: I got sent home from a Baptist lock-in in the eighth grade for what the youth pastor called *interpretive dance*. Two: I have been bitten by a horse in a full pageant gown, and I *placed*. Three: I have never been to Oklahoma.”
“What’s interpretive dance?” Kevin asks.
“It’s whatever the youth pastor says it is, Kevin. That’s the lesson.”
“Three,” says the van, in four voices.
“You go to Oklahoma by accident,” Laney says, unbothered. “It’s like a cold.”

Margot doesn’t wait either. “One: I have two hundred and eleven pages of field notes on the third floor of Delgado. Two: I was asked to leave a sorority’s rush week for taking minutes. Three: I didn’t mind.”
“Three,” Theo says. “You minded.”
“Two. They asked me back.” Margot turns a page of San Bernardino County. “I declined. The data had saturated.”
Kevin, after a moment: “What were the minutes of?”
“Who cried in the bathroom, and when, and whose sweater she was wearing. It’s a kinship system. They just call it sisterhood.”
From the way-back, Laney, wounded and fascinated: “Which house?”
“I’d never tell you that.”

Theo gives himself the floor with a hand on his heart. “I have been on a yacht with a Kennedy. I have been seasick on a yacht with a Kennedy. The yacht was a hundred and twelve feet, a Feadship, out of Hyannis, forty-one tons, teak decks, and the Kennedy was a second cousin by marriage in a pair of —”
“The tonnage,” Margot says.
Theo closes his mouth. “I hadn’t even got to his loafers.”
He turns farther round in his seat, past Margot, past Jack’s headrest, to the way-back. “Broussard.”
Behind Jack and to the left, where she has ridden since Marisol: “I’ll pass, Theo.”
Theo waits. She lets him wait.
“I hear I’m unreliable,” Lena says.
Nobody laughs. Kevin checks his mirror and finds nothing in it he wants. Margot’s highlighter stops halfway across Rialto.
“House rules,” Theo starts, “a pass costs you —”
“Sugar,” Laney says. “Let it go.”
Jack watches a Costco go by his window, and the long beige wall of the one after it.

Theo pulls his visor down. In the little mirror on the back of it, from where Jack sits, there is a slice of the way-back: copper hair, a pair of sunglasses, Laney’s face looking straight into the mirror at Theo’s. Laney’s eyes drop to the pink BlackBerry in her lap, and she gets very interested in it. Theo flips the visor up.
He comes round on Jack with all his teeth. “Costigan. Father Jack. Two truths, one lie. Dazzle the Inland Empire.”

choices.text: “My grandmother calls me Giacomino. I gave a marionberry pie a four. I’ve read all of Chesterton.”
response: Margot, without looking up: “Nobody has read all of Chesterton. Chesterton hasn’t.”
“It’s a lot of books,” Kevin agrees.

Theo awards the point to Margot, who accepts it like a parking validation. The game limps on past Redlands with the floor open and no takers, and up the long grade past Yucaipa, and it dies at the top of the pass at Beaumont.

choices.text: “I’ve met Tony Romo. My father drove me twenty-four hundred miles to college. I can name every pope since Leo the Thirteenth.”
response: Laney doesn’t let him finish the sentence. “Nobody’s met Tony Romo. He’s from *Wisconsin*.”
“Name the popes,” Kevin says.

He names them, with the numbers, the way he learned them in the fourth grade, standing up: Leo, Pius, Benedict, Pius, Pius, John, Paul, John Paul, John Paul. He gets to Benedict the Sixteenth just as they top the pass at Beaumont, and Kevin says, “That’s correct,” as though he had been holding the list.

choices.text: “Pass. I’m driving West Texas. I’m saving my lies.”
response: “That’s two passes,” Theo says.
“It’s a trend,” says Margot. “I’ll allow it.”

Theo faces front and studies the Inland Empire as if it had personally let him down. The game dies at the top of the pass at Beaumont with nobody’s lie on the table, and the road tips down toward Banning, and the desert opens out ahead of them, brown and enormous under the overcast.

body: The wind comes down the San Gorgonio Pass hard enough to lean on. It flattens the creosote along the frontage road, throws grit across the pumps, and rips the sliding door out of Margot’s hand the second she unlatches it. Kevin’s card says gas at half a tank, and at half a tank exactly Kevin put his signal on, and so they are here: a gas station, a diner, a lot full of RVs, and beyond the lot the dinosaurs, standing in the wind. A brontosaurus the length of a motel, concrete, weathered, its neck going up into the gray and its tail coming down to the asphalt. Behind it a tyrannosaur six stories tall with its little arms up and its mouth open on a row of teeth, roaring at the interstate.

Kevin takes the pump. The rest of them go across the lot because it is there. Theo holds his iPhone up at the tyrannosaur and takes its picture, and then takes it again with Laney under it doing a pageant wave, wrist, wrist, elbow, elbow, into the wind, her hair going straight sideways off her head. Margot has her map pinned under one arm so it won’t leave for Arizona without her.

The gift shop is inside the brontosaurus. You go in by a door in its flank, under its ribs, and inside are rubber dinosaurs and dinosaur T-shirts and a shelf of books about the Flood, and placards along the walls in careful lettering that ask the visitor to consider how old he thinks the earth is, and why he thinks so, and who told him. The woman at the register, in a fleece vest, says good morning to each of them as they come in out of the wind, and asks where they’re headed, and when Laney says New Orleans she says, “Well, God bless the Saints, then,” and gives her a sticker.

Margot stops in the doorway and takes it all in. “A young-earth gift shop,” she says, very softly, “inside a Jurassic misunderstanding. I’m home.” She explains to Kevin, who has come in from the pump to see, that there is no such animal as a brontosaurus — it’s an apatosaurus that spent most of a century wearing the wrong head — and goes in reverently, like a woman entering a cathedral she intends to write up.

She finds Jack at the postcard rack by the back wall and stands beside him in front of a placard, and reads it over twice, and turns to him with something close to joy. “Defend this,” she says. “Professionally.”
At the other end of the shop, by the T-shirts, Kevin has asked Lena something too, low, with his hands in his quarter-zip.

“Augustine already did,” Jack says. “He says it’s a disgrace when somebody who doesn’t believe hears a Christian talking nonsense about the natural world. Because the guy knows better, and he laughs, and then why would he believe you about the resurrection.”

And at the far end of the shop, at the same time, at the same speed, in her own words: “— Augustine says it’s a scandal when a Christian talks nonsense about the earth and the stars to a man who knows better, because the man laughs at you, Kevin, and after that he won’t listen to you about anything that matters —”

They both hear it. They both stop. Across a rack of T-shirts, a tyrannosaur in sunglasses and a brontosaurus with CABAZON across its ribs, Jack and Lena look at each other, a glare apiece, and look away.

Beside him Margot closes her mouth on whatever she had ready. “Well,” she says. None of it has carried as far as the register, where the woman in the fleece is showing Laney which postcards have the sunset on them and which ones have the snow on San Jacinto, and saying that both are true, depending on the day.

Outside, the wind has the flags on the gas station snapping straight out. Theo and Laney have stationed themselves under the tyrannosaur’s feet, directly on the way back to the van, and are having a conversation loud enough to reach the pumps.
“It’s fascinating,” Theo is saying, “how two people can remember the *same phone call* completely differently.”
“I read about it in *Cosmo*,” Laney says. “It happens to *couples*.”
Jack walks past them to the van without breaking stride. Behind him the gift-shop door bangs, and a pair of boots goes the other way across the asphalt, toward the restrooms.
Kevin comes out of the brontosaurus behind him on his way back to the pump, and stops square in front of the two of them. Over the wind it carries fine.
“Respectfully,” Kevin says. “Leave it alone.”
“We’re discussing *paleontology*,” Theo says.
“Leave the paleontology alone.”

Jack stands at the hatch with his hands in the Carhartt and the wind in his ears. Across the back glass, in white: WHO DAT · 2 DAYS. The 2 is new since the pumps. Somebody has wiped out the 3 with a fingertip and made a 2 over the smear, and the white is still wet; the wind is drying it while he watches, the bottom stroke going dull first.

choices.text: *A postcard of the T. rex, for Danny.*
response: He goes back in through the brontosaurus’s side. The postcard is a tyrannosaur against a blue sky Cabazon hasn’t seen all day, roaring, twenty-five cents. The woman in the fleece gives him change for a dollar and tells him to drive safe. He doesn’t write anything on it. It goes flat into the back of the book, against the inside cover.
On the 10 east the windmills come up through his window, on the slopes past Cabazon, a thousand of them, white, turning all together in a wind none of them can feel through the glass.

choices.text: *A plastic brontosaurus for Rosie, with a Latin name on the box.*
response: He goes back in for it. It’s three ninety-nine, green, with *BRONTOSAURUS EXCELSUS* across the window of the box in yellow. Margot takes it out of his hand in the aisle and turns it over.
“That’s not a real genus.”
“It is to an eight-year-old.”
“That’s how it starts,” Margot says, and gives it back, and goes to pay for her own, which is a stegosaurus.

choices.text: *Nothing. Back to the van.*
response: He slides the door open and gets in, middle right, out of the wind. Kevin is back at the pump, doing the windshield in long even strokes against the gusts, and when he comes around the hood he raps a knuckle on Jack’s glass. “Good man.”
The rest of them come back one at a time and the doors slide and slam, Lena last, with her hood up against the grit.

s04.slug: FRIDAY · 1:15 PM · I-10 EAST, BLYTHE → THE COLORADO RIVER
body: Jack wakes at Blythe with his face against the window and the sun full on it, the windmills two and a half hours gone. Out in the desert, for no reason the last hundred miles have offered, there are fields: alfalfa as green as a pool table, irrigation ditches running full and ruler-straight beside it, a stand of date palms around a farmhouse with a pickup parked under them and both its doors open.
The RAZR in his lap has two from Burnaby.

body.text: light rain. 8 degrees
forecast: rain tomorrow

body: A weather report, and a minute behind it a forecast. Eight degrees is about forty-six. It’s raining on her in Canada, and by her own rules she’s already missing him tomorrow. He doesn’t answer yet. He’d like to have some weather of his own first.

The Colorado comes up under the van green, which he wasn’t ready for, with reeds along both banks and a row of aluminum boats nosed in under an RV park, the river that cut the Grand Canyon looking like it has never heard of the place. A sign at the end of the bridge welcomes them to Arizona.
“It’s two-twenty in Arizona,” Kevin says. “We lost an hour. I’m logging it.” He holds his thumbnail on the hour button of the dash clock until the clock agrees with the state.

Ehrenberg is the first exit, and Kevin takes it. He tops off, because “Arizona’s thirty cents cheaper. That’s not a preference,” and has the hood up before the pump clicks. He pulls the dipstick, wipes it on a blue shop towel, pushes it home, pulls it again and holds it up to the sun. Frank Costigan loses to a pre-med again, in a second state.

The receipt comes back to the van with Kevin. He hands it in to Margot, and Margot reaches it back over her headrest into the way-back, where a pen writes it down on a legal pad. It travels the left side of the van and never comes near Jack’s, which is the system, and the system works.
He texts his father.

Theo takes the keys at the pump. Kevin gets in on the passenger side and leans across to fix Theo’s mirrors, both of them, while Theo looks for the ignition on the wrong side of the wheel. Margot stays where she is, beside Jack, with La Paz County printed out on her knees in yellow highlighter.
Past the truck scales the RAZR buzzes against his leg.

body: Jack shuts the phone and puts it in his shirt pocket, flat, where he’ll feel the next one come in.
“Sixty-four,” Kevin says. “Sixty-five. Hold it there.” Ahead the desert opens out flat to a line of bare brown mountains, and the needle holds. “That’s beautiful, Theo.”

s05.slug: FRIDAY · 5:05 PM · I-10 EAST, PHOENIX → THE GILA RIVER — EIGHT
body: Kevin has turned the mix off. He did it at the Phoenix city limits, ejected the disc into its sleeve and said, “Atmosphere,” and since then the Odyssey has had the tires, the fan in the dash and Kevin.

Theo has it through downtown and into the Broadway Curve at Friday rush hour, eight lanes of Phoenix going home with the low sun behind them flashing off every rear window ahead, and Kevin talks him across it like a delivery. “You’ve got a gap. You’ve got a gap. Breathe. Signal. Okay — *now*.” The Odyssey goes in between a cement truck and a Camry. Kevin sits back. “And we’re in. Everybody’s healthy.”
“I was born at Cedars-Sinai,” Theo says, “with less coaching.”
In Chandler, Margot’s Nokia buzzes in the milk crate at her feet. She reads it, puts it back, and says, without malice, “Eight now.”
Kevin’s eyes come up to the mirror. Margot answers him anyway, in ascending order of reliability, with Maricopa County open on her knees.

“The one where the dog gives an interview. That’s Doug’s. Kenzie Rourke’s, in which somebody threw a glass. The Forum table’s, in which Caleb says Hale chaired it like a Lambeth Conference. The Classics department’s, which still has a chorus and is now about Thucydides. Priya’s, which has a form number. Joey Abruzzo’s, which I’ve only heard from two floors away.” She turns a page of Arizona. “Becca’s is a refusal to have one. She said she wasn’t there and she isn’t going to be. I’m counting it.”

She lets a semi go by on the left. “And the eighth, by Nokia, just now. I’m told Julian heard about it and said nothing.” She looks out at Chandler. “That one’s my favorite. It’s the only accurate one.”
From the way-back, directly behind Jack, Laney says, “Margot. *Hush*, or I’m telling them version nine.”
“There isn’t a version nine.”
“Not yet there isn’t.”
Margot turns a page. “Kevin hasn’t contributed one.”
“I don’t have the information,” Kevin says, with his eyes on Theo’s speedometer.

After that the Odyssey is miserable in four directions. Theo tries a pitch on a billboard past the last of the subdivisions, a personal-injury lawyer forty feet wide with his arms folded — “Open on a mustache. A man in Mesa has been wronged, and he has a *feeling* about it —” and lets it go, and drives. Laney opens a bag of Twizzlers and says, “Isn’t this nice. Isn’t this just the nicest,” and eats them one after another behind her sunglasses. Kevin tells everybody what a great car this is, and at the next exit what great mileage it gets, and at the one after that he stops. Margot reads the counties.

Jack was at the original. So were Theo and Laney, up front and right behind him, and not one of the three of them corrects a word of any of the eight. The Gila River goes under them a few miles on, a quarter mile of sand and tamarisk with a river somewhere in it and a sign to say so.

From the way-back, left side, nothing. He and Lena say nothing at all, across the reservation and the long flat after it, while the sun comes around into the right-hand windows and lies across Margot’s maps.

Past Casa Grande a green sign comes up for the Picacho Peak exit, and beyond it the peak itself stands up out of the flat, one black broken tooth against the west, with the last of the sun burning along its edges.

s06.slug: FRIDAY · 6:00 PM · PICACHO PEAK, A TRUCK STOP OFF I-10 — THE CALL
body: The sun is going down behind Picacho Peak. From the pump island the mountain has gone to a cutout of itself, a black crown of rock with the light coming around its edges, and the sky over it runs orange at the bottom and red above that, and straight overhead it’s already blue. On the slope below, the saguaros stand in the last of the light with their arms up. Out on the interstate the trucks gear down for the exit one after another, a long falling groan of engine and then the gasp of the air brakes, and the wind comes across the flat with diesel in it, and hot asphalt giving back the day, and something green and resinous out in the scrub that Ohio never taught him the name of.

GAS AT HALF A TANK, NOT A QUARTER is taped to the dash, and the gauge said half at Casa Grande, so here they are. Theo, who drove them in, has never pumped gasoline. He stands at the pump holding the nozzle in both hands with its business end pointed at the Odyssey from a respectful distance, and Kevin stands beside him with the squeegee out of the bucket, dripping on his shoes. “In the hole. Push it in. Now the handle.” Theo looks at the nozzle. “The handle. *The handle*, Theo.”
The pump starts. Theo goes still all over and watches the dollars on the display go round a good deal faster than the gallons. “Kevin,” he says. “It’s *loud*.”

Margot comes out of the store with a stick of jerky in a paper sleeve and a postcard of a saguaro, and holds her free hand out for the keys, and Theo, without letting go of anything, gets them into it. Laney is on the curb under the store’s awning in her sunglasses, one leg out straight in front of her, reaching for the toe of her boot and saying *ow* at intervals. In the open side door of the way-back Lena sits with the legal pad on her knee and the day’s receipts under its clip, writing.

The RAZR goes off in his shirt pocket, against his chest. On the little outside screen: SKYE (MISFIT). He has it open before the second ring, and leans back against the van with his free hand up on the roof rail, still warm from the sun.
“I’ve been met,” Skye says. No hello. “At the bottom of the escalator. A man in a fleece, holding a sign, and the sign said CASSIE.”
“Did you go to him?”

“Almost didn’t. I stood at the top and thought, good, she’s got a ride.” Paper rustles on her end, close to the phone. “I’ve never been met by my *character* before. I didn’t know what to say to him. I said, ‘She’s running late.’ He drove me anyway.”
Jack laughs into the wind. “How’s Burnaby?”
“Kansas with Starbucks.” Behind her a man is calling out a scene number. “Landed by lunch. Wardrobe by two. And Jack. Wardrobe went through my bags.”
“And?”

“They found your shirt. The costume lady held it up by the shoulders and said, *Whose is this*, and I said a boy’s, and she said *obviously*. They’re keeping the salsa on the cuff. They say it’s character. It got the part. It’s recurring. Cassie wears it in the porch scene, over the cardigan, with the sleeves down over her hands.” She lowers her voice, in a trailer in Canada, for him. “I wore you all afternoon. Wardrobe thinks I’m method.”
Jack looks down at the concrete of the pump island, at an old dark stain on it the shape of Lake Erie, and the back of his neck goes hot in the wind. “Is it method?”

“It’s extremely method. Ask my elbows.” She does Corinne down the line from Burnaby, consonants and all. “*Skye.* The skin person called the hotel. About your *elbows*. Cassie has *indoor* elbows. Are those *indoor* elbows?” And she’s herself again. “They’re outdoor elbows, Jack. I’ve been surfing on them. There’s going to be a meeting.”
“What about the geese?”
“The geese are real. I was right. Labradors. There was one by the stages this morning, standing on a parking bumper, and it watched me the entire way to the door like it had read the sides.”
“Did it have notes?”
“One note. It was *hiss*.”
“Pop says to tell the TV one hello. Ma says Canada’s cold.”
“The TV one.” She tries it in her mouth. “I’m going to be the TV one on Glenwood Avenue for the rest of my life, aren’t I.”
“Pretty much.”

“Good. It’s eight degrees. I have a coat she’d approve of. It’s long, and it has a lining.” The rustle again, and a long creak, somebody sitting down on something that doesn’t want her to. “I’m in a trailer. It says CASSIE on the door, so I’m subletting. I have a space heater and the sides and a cup of tea that tastes like a hotel. I’m tired, Jack. Actually tired. It’s the good kind. I haven’t had it in a while.”
“Six a.m. call tomorrow,” she says. “I’m the one with the call time now.”
Jack’s hand tightens on the roof rail.
“Where are you?” she says. “Don’t say Texas. You’re not in Texas.”
“Arizona. A truck stop. I’m standing on an oil stain the shape of Lake Erie.”
“Close enough for a margin. Read me a rude one.”

Hale’s *Moviegoer* comes out of his back pocket one-handed. It falls open where the print is, lying face-down between the pages with its back to the sky, and he keeps his thumb on it and pages on past with his other fingers to a passage where Binx is talking about making money, and about how much he enjoys it. Beside it in the margin is Hale’s small upright pencil.
“Okay,” he says. “A margin. Binx, on the subject of money.” And he reads it out across a pump island in Pinal County: “*Spoken like a man who has never paid for anything.*”
She laughs. It comes down the line out of Canada with the sound left in, hoarse at the edges from the day, and behind it he can make out the fan of a space heater in a trailer in Burnaby.
“He’s right,” she says, when she has her breath. “He’s right, and it’s a terrible note. You can’t play a man who’s never paid for anything. You can only play one who thinks the bill hasn’t come yet.”
“That should go in under his.”
“In pen. Initialed.”

Around him the truck stop does its best not to listen. Theo holds the handle in and watches the dollars. Kevin does the windshield top to bottom in long strokes and moves around to the side glass. Margot reads the back of her own postcard. Laney has her forehead down on her knee. At the side door the pen has stopped.
“Okay,” Skye says. “Tell Kevin sixty-five.”
“He knows.”
“Tell him anyway. Tell Margot I’ve started her notes. Tell Theo —” She thinks about it. “Ted. *Behave*.”
Outside her trailer a woman’s voice calls for Cassie. “That’s me,” Skye says. “I mean that’s her. I have to go be indoors.”

response: “Love you,” he says.

He says it at the volume he says everything else, at a pump island in Arizona with five people inside twenty feet of him, and doesn’t lower it for any of them. “Say it in Texas too,” Skye says. “Bye, Lake Erie.”
The hinge of the RAZR complains as it shuts. He puts the phone back in his shirt pocket and gives the stop its messages in order, down the island. “Kevin. Sixty-five.”
Kevin, the squeegee up against the side glass: “*Not sixty-six.*”
“Margot. She’s started your notes.”
Margot is in the driver’s seat with the door open and the jerky in her teeth. She takes it out to say, “Tell her I’ll be the judge.”
“Theo. Ted. Behave.”
Theo gets the nozzle back into its cradle on the third try and steps away from it. “Callender has never once told me to behave and meant it.”
On the curb Laney brings her sunglasses down her nose, and over the top of them she looks at Jack until Margot turns the key; and behind him the van’s slide doors roll shut, one after another.

“Hang on.” Her mouth goes away from the phone, and he hears her say it to the trailer, gravely, and wait. She comes back. “She says she will. She says it’s the warmest thing in the trailer.” The voice outside calls again. “Bye, Lake Erie.”

The RAZR is still warm in his hand when he leans down to the driver’s window, where Margot has the seat run up to the wheel and every mirror already wrong for everyone but her. He gives her the news through the window. “She’s started your notes.”
Margot slots the postcard into the visor. “Tell her I’ll be the judge.”
Across the hood Kevin sets the squeegee to the windshield and raises his eyebrows at Jack, and Jack says, “Sixty-five.”
“*Not sixty-six*,” Kevin says through the glass.
“Theo. Ted says behave.”
Theo gets the nozzle back into its cradle on the third try. “Callender has never once told me to behave and meant it.”
Laney’s sunglasses come down. She looks at him over them from the curb, and gets up, and dusts off the back of her jeans; and the slide doors go behind him, one and then the other.

“Twelve and a quarter,” she says at once. “I’m counting the parking lot.” Under the heater’s fan he hears her breathe out, the long one people do at the end of a day. “Me too. Go get in your van. Bye, Lake Erie.”
Kevin is already waiting at the end of the island when the RAZR shuts, the squeegee in his fist. “Did she say sixty-five?”
“She said sixty-five.”
“*Not sixty-six.*” Kevin drops the squeegee in the bucket. “What else?”
“Margot, she’s started your notes.”
Margot, behind the wheel with the door open, is getting her jerky out of its sleeve. “Tell her I’ll be the judge.”
“And Ted’s to behave.”

s06a.slug: FRIDAY · 6:30 PM · I-10 EAST, PICACHO → MARANA — ONE SENTENCE
body: Lena was in the way-back before anybody else had a door open, the legal pad shut on her pen. Now Margot has the wheel, both hands on it where the driver’s manual puts them, the needle laid on sixty-five and kept there. Kevin rides shotgun with the map light on and Pinal County open on his knee. Theo has come back to the middle-left beside Jack with his camel coat folded across his lap, and Laney is in the way-back behind Jack, and Lena is behind Theo, in the corner of the van farthest from anything.

Behind them the peak has gone flat black against a sky that is still orange along the bottom and navy everywhere else. The saguaros along the right-of-way go dark against it, every one of them with its arms up, and the orange thins to a line along the mountains, and then the line goes, and it’s the dashboard and the road and the red lights of a cattle truck far ahead. The van hasn’t said a word since the pump. The tires have, and the fan in the dash, and once Kevin, turning a page of Arizona under the little light: “Marana.” Its lights come up ahead out of the flat, low and yellow: a truck stop, a water tower, a long lit fence around something agricultural.

The call is still on him. He can feel where the RAZR was warm against his ear, and he has her laugh, the real one, with the trailer’s space heater going behind it in Burnaby, and *Bye, Lake Erie*, which is going to be in his head till Texas. Up front Theo’s iPod sits dark in the cup holder with its transmitter. Behind Jack, Laney’s BlackBerry throws a little light up onto the ceiling, and goes out, and comes on again. The book is in his lap with his hand on it.
From the way-back, to her own window, Lena says, “You always did read a margin well.”

It isn’t loud. It doesn’t have to be. There’s no Kevin in it and no Laney: nine days since Hale’s, and the first sentence she has put in the air for him comes straight across the van with no name on the envelope, and there’s no question in the car whose it is. Behind Jack, Laney’s head comes up off the window. Beside him Theo shuts his eyes.

Jack hears the pump in it: Hale’s pencil, and his own voice going across the island to a trailer in Burnaby while five people checked tire pressure they had already checked. The pen stopped at the side door while he read. He heard it stop.

choices.text: “She asked.”
choices.key: Past Picacho Lena spoke to you for the first time since Hale’s: you always did read a margin well. You told her Skye asked.
response: “She asked,” he says, over his left shoulder.
“She asks for a lot,” Lena says.
Marana comes up level with them and starts to go by on the right, the truck stop and the tower and the long lit fence, and none of it is any help. He turns around the rest of the way.

choices.text: “Kevin, tell her thank you.”
choices.key: Past Picacho Lena spoke to you for the first time since Hale’s: you always did read a margin well. You told Kevin to tell her thank you. Kevin said no.
response: “Kevin,” he says. “Tell her thank you.”
Kevin doesn’t turn around. His hand is still up on the map light, and he says it without turning his head, perfectly pleasant, the first relay he has turned down all day. “No.”
“He’s not a switchboard, Costigan,” Lena says. “He said so.”
So it’s Costigan, then, out loud, in the van, with Marana going by. Jack turns around in his seat to have a look at her.

choices.text: *Say nothing.*
choices.key: Past Picacho Lena spoke to you for the first time since Hale’s: you always did read a margin well. You said nothing. She went on anyway.
response: He says nothing. He watches Marana come up out of the dark on the right and lets her have the window.
She doesn’t need him. “It’s a talent,” she says, in the same tone, conversational, a woman remarking on the scenery. “You should do it for everybody. I hear you do.”
And his head comes around, all on its own, over his left shoulder.

choices.text: “You’d know.”
choices.key: Past Picacho Lena spoke to you for the first time since Hale’s: you always did read a margin well. You said: you’d know.
response: “You’d know,” he says.
He hears it go in. He doesn’t have to turn around to hear it. Behind Theo the way-back goes still.
She lets it lie there while Marana’s lights go by, the truck stop and the tower and the long fence sliding back past her window. When Marana is behind them she starts, and she has plenty.

s07.slug: FRIDAY · 7:00 PM · I-10 EAST, TUCSON — THE CAPTION
body: Tucson is a grid of lights laid flat on both sides of the interstate, streetlights running off in dead-straight lines toward mountains that are only a darker part of the dark now, the Catalinas, with a red light blinking on a tower somewhere along the top. Margot holds sixty-five through all of it. To fight in this van Jack has to turn in his seat over his left shoulder and talk past the side of Theo’s headrest to the corner of the way-back, with the shoulder belt sawing at his collarbone, and that is how he fights it.
“Some of us got our margins read to us too,” Lena says. “I didn’t know it was a *repertoire*.”
“It’s a book, Broussard.”

“It’s a *bit*. It’s a bit you do.” In the light off the cattle truck they’re passing he can see her sitting very straight, the legal pad face-down on her knees, both hands flat on it. “And she’s so good at bits. *We agree on each other.*” She reads him the caption in no voice at all, the way you’d read the side of a cereal box. “*Not just friends from school.* And the little heart. Less than three. She did the arithmetic for four hundred people.”

body.text: “And then you made it your *face*. And she wrote under it, for everybody: *happy looks good on you.*” The same no voice, every word of it, like she’s read it more than once.

body: “She can’t have a sandwich,” Lena says, “without telling four hundred people.”
Behind him Laney says, low, “Lena.”
“I’m talking about the *weather*, Laney. I’m making conversation with the man. We’ve got fourteen hundred miles.”

“You want the caption?” He’s round as far as the belt lets him. “I’ll give you the caption. They had me in a house in the Palisades full of people who’d paid to be there for a senator from a state I can’t vote in and wouldn’t if I could, with her name on a banner and a man with a camera at the foot of the steps. She didn’t walk me out. She could have. She stood me up in the middle of it and asked every one of them why they thought I was wrong, and then she shut up and let me answer, one after another, all night, in a room that was supposed to be theirs. And when Corinne wanted the picture, me under Boxer’s name, she wouldn’t post it. She blew a raspberry and posted us at a taquería instead. So nobody back home opens a computer and thinks I stood for something I don’t.” He hears his voice go up the inside of the van and doesn’t bring it down. “That’s what she posted. That’s your sandwich.”
“So she *edited* you,” Lena says.
“She *argued* me. In a room that paid to watch me lose. You know the difference. You’ve got her caption by heart, you can work it out.”

“It’s a *caption*, Costigan. I’ve got the Exsultet by heart, and it runs a good deal longer, and nobody’s made me a deacon.” She doesn’t let him have the laugh, if there was one in it. “If it was real, why put it up? Real keeps. You don’t have to tell four hundred people about a thing that’s real. It’ll still be there in the morning.”

“Because somebody else was going to put up the other one. That’s how it goes when people have been taking your picture since you were a kid. You get there first, or you get the one they pick.” He has the seat back in his fist. “They built her that window, Lena. She didn’t. And you’ve got your face pressed up against it every night, reading the comments.”
“I don’t have to read the comments. I hear them in the Fishbowl. You’re *Mystery Guy*. You’ve got a following. Doug Pruitt says it across the Commons like it’s your name.”
“I didn’t ask to be anybody’s mystery.”
“No. You just stood where the camera was.”

“And you didn’t?” It’s out of him before he has decided anything. “Nine days, Lena. Nine days you didn’t speak to me, and you did it where everybody could watch you do it. In the Fishbowl. In the Commons, past Doug Pruitt, with your chin up. Last night in a parking lot, through Kevin, with five people loading coolers and pretending they couldn’t hear. You don’t give somebody the silent treatment alone in your room. There’s no point. You do it in front of a crowd, so they can see how hard you’re not talking to him.” It comes out the way he has been saying it in his head since Hale’s, every word in its place. “That’s a caption too. You just didn’t have to write it down.”
For a mile there is only the road. Then: “I didn’t have anything to say to you.”
“You had plenty. You said every word of it to Kevin.”
“Kevin,” Lena says, “listens.”

body.text: “You don’t care,” Lena says. “You said so. Loud enough for the hatch.” She waits. “Not unless it’s got a caption on it.”
“You’re not a subscriber,” Lena says. “You said so. Loud enough for the hatch.” She waits. “Not unless it’s got a caption on it.”
“You don’t care,” Lena says. “You asked her why she’d think you would. Loud enough for the hatch.” She waits. “Not unless it’s got a caption on it.”

body: “That one,” Jack says, “I meant.”
“Good,” Lena says. “Then we agree on something. Write it on a napkin. She’ll post it.”

“You’d know about writing things down.” He nods at the pad under her hands. “Every receipt in this van is under that clip. Kevin’s gas. Margot’s jerky. Laney’s Twizzlers. You’ve kept books on five people since the Rincon and you haven’t said thank you to one of them. That’s what you do instead of talking to people, Lena. You keep their receipts.”
“Somebody has to know what things cost.”
“You know what everything costs,” he says. “You’ve just never once paid for anything out loud.”
It’s Hale’s pencil, turned around, and he watches it land. Her hands go flat on the pad. “You have no idea,” she says, very evenly, “what I pay.”

In the middle-left Theo has turned his face to his window as though there were something out there in the dark besides Tucson’s last car dealerships going by, and behind Jack, Laney has taken her sunglasses off her head and put them on, at seven at night, in a van.
Up front Kevin turns round in his seat with Arizona slipping off his knee. “Respectfully, could we —”
“*No*,” say Jack and Lena.

Kevin faces front. He reaches up and switches off the map light, and keeps his hand on it a little while in the dark, and then takes the hand down and leaves the light off, and sits there with Pima County on his knee where he can’t read it.

choices.text: “She posted tacos so a fundraiser couldn’t use me. You want to tell me what’s fake about that?”
response: “Tell me what’s fake about it. Go ahead. She posted tacos so a fundraiser couldn’t use me.”

“Nothing,” Lena says. “Nothing in the world. It’s the most sincere marketing I’ve ever seen.” She tips her head at him in the dark. “She marketed *you*, Jack. To you. And look at you. You bought it twice.”

choices.text: “You’ve been keeping up with her page, then.”
response: “You’ve kept up with her page, then. Good to know somebody reads it.”
“Everybody keeps up with her page. That’s what a page is *for*.” She doesn’t miss a stride. “A diary, you have to steal out of a drawer. She leaves hers out on the porch with the lights on.”

choices.text: “Fine. She posts. She’s posted since she was a kid. For years the network did it for her.”
response: “Fine. She posts. She’s posted since she was a kid. For years the network did it for her, and she didn’t get a vote.”

It stops her. He watches it stop her, in the corner of the way-back, her mouth closing on whatever she had ready next. It doesn’t last. “Then she’s had a lot of practice,” Lena says, and it comes back harder for the stop, and he is sorry he gave her anything.

choices.text: “You read the rest of the screen in the lounge. I watched you shut the laptop.”
response: “You read the rest of the screen in the lounge,” he says. “I was in the door. I watched you shut the laptop.”
The way-back goes silent, with nothing in the silence at all. When she speaks it’s level. “I shut it because Laney had crumbs in the keyboard.”
“I did *not*,” Laney says.
It’s the cruelest thing he has said to her tonight, and he knows it because it worked.

s08.slug: FRIDAY · 8:10 PM · I-10 EAST, TEXAS CANYON — WORD FOR WORD
body: Texas Canyon comes up in the headlights all at once, in Arizona, of all places: boulders, round and gray, heaped on both sides of the road taller than the van, one balanced on another balanced on a third, as if something enormous had set them down in piles and forgotten to come back for them. The lights sweep them and let them go, and they’re gone behind.

“You’re still telling it wrong,” Lena says. “To everybody. Kenzie Rourke stopped me outside the Fishbowl on Tuesday to tell me she’s on my *side*.” Lena says *side* as if Kenzie had handed it to her wet. “I don’t want a side. I want it to have happened the way it happened.”
“Doug Pruitt asked me Monday if you threw a jam jar at Hale’s dog.”
“I did not throw a —”
“I know. I told him you threw it at me.”
“Well, that’s the one he tells now. Thank you. I’m a *menace* in the Classics department.”
Margot’s eyes come up to the mirror and go back to the road.

body.text: “There are eight versions of me calling you a liar, Lena,” Jack says, “and in seven of them I’m right.”
body.else: “There are eight versions of Wednesday, Lena,” Jack says, “and in seven of them I’m right.”

body: “Then say it right.”
“I can do it word for word.”
“So can I.”

And they do. Both of them, at the same moment, every line of it, hers and his, in two voices over the road noise, her Louisiana and his Ohio laid one on top of the other like two parishes saying the Creed:
“Will you be around after? Monday night. Nine, ten.”
“Probably not. I’ve got a thing.”
“Okay. Then call me after. Eat something first.”
“I haven’t been fair to him, Jack. I’ve known it a while. I’m going to fix it.”

body.text: “Okay.”
“He’s a good guy, Lena. He deserves that.”
“Why are you telling me?”
“Fix it how? Write him a song?”

body: It comes out even. The same words in the same order, down to the *and*s, and when it’s over the van has gone so quiet under it that the fan in the dash sounds loud.
Margot, driving: “Those were the same words.”
“Then you know what I said,” Lena says.
“I know exactly what you said.”
“So tell them what it meant,” Lena says. “Go on. Tell the van.”
“You tell them. It was your call.”
Margot drives. Neither of them tells anybody anything.
“You *know* —” She stops. Whatever was behind it she puts back. “Who taught you to do it so pretty? You had it by heart. You had the *pauses*.”
“I said it word for word to one person,” Jack says, “once, and that was Theo. Because he asked me to.”
“*Laney* made me do it,” Lena says. “Twice. At the *mailboxes*.”
His head comes round to the left, to Theo, at the same moment hers comes round to the right, to Laney.
“Anthropology,” says Theo.
“Sugar,” Laney says, “I was making *conversation*.”
Margot keeps her eyes on the road. “I’ve asked nobody anything. I’d like that minuted.”
“I said leave it alone,” Kevin says, without turning around. “In January.”

Margot takes one hand off the wheel, which Jack has not seen her do all night, and drives a mile of Cochise County that way while she rubs her eyes under her glasses with the other. “I should have taken the train,” she tells the windshield.
From the way-back, in a very small voice, Laney says, “We could play Two Truths.” Two Truths does not get played.

It doesn’t last, whatever it was. Her eyes go to Theo and come back, and Jack gets there a second behind her, the other way round: if Theo had to ask, Theo had a reason to. If Laney made her do it twice —
“What did you tell him it *was*?” she says.
“What did you tell *her*?”
“You told Theo I —”
“You told Laney I —”
And there it stops, his and hers.

body.text: “You’re a liar, Costigan,” Lena says. Not at a table this time. Close, in the dark, with nowhere for anybody to go. “And now there are witnesses who were *told*.”
body.else: “Then one of us is lying to a best friend,” Lena says, close, in the dark, with nowhere for anybody to go, “and I know which.”

body: “Twice,” Jack says. “At the mailboxes. You needed two takes, Lena? For *Laney*?”
“And Theo got it the first time.” She doesn’t look at Theo; she doesn’t have to. “Theo believes anything, if you sound tired enough.”

body.text: “You love a witness,” Jack says. “You called me a liar across Hale’s table with the plates still out and his dog underneath it. You didn’t wait for the porch. You didn’t wait for the car. You needed the room for it, Lena. You needed it to *count*.”
body.else: “You love a witness,” Jack says. “You asked me about a Facebook status across Hale’s table with the plates still out and his dog underneath it. You didn’t wait for the porch. You didn’t wait for the car. You needed the room for it, Lena. You needed it to *count*.”

body: “I didn’t *plan* it.” It comes up out of her hot. “It came out of me at a dinner table, in front of God and the dog, because it was *true*. That’s the difference between me and her, Jack. Nothing comes out of her she didn’t plan.”
“Everything comes out of you,” he says. “That’s not honesty. That’s weather.”
She doesn’t answer that. She goes back to the call.

choices.text: “Same words. Every one. You want them again?”
response: “Same words. Every one. You want them again? I’ll do yours this time. I’ve got your part.”
“Once was plenty,” Lena says. “I was there for the first one.”

choices.text: “Two people heard the same call. Maybe nobody’s lying. Maybe —”
response: “Two people heard the same call,” he says. “Maybe nobody’s lying. Maybe —”

“Don’t you *dare* be reasonable at me in a car.” She’s on top of it before he gets to the end, and she doesn’t let him have the end. But a rest area goes by on the right with its lights on, and in the light her face says she heard the half he got out.

choices.text: “Laney took notes? Did she bring them? Laney, did you bring the notes?”
response: He turns the other way, to the seat behind his. “Laney took notes? Did she bring them? Laney. Did you bring the notes?”
“I will put you out of this car,” Laney says, “at seventy miles an hour.”
“Sixty-five,” says Kevin, from the front.
Lena hasn’t laughed. Lena is waiting for him to come back round to her, and when he does she is right where he left her.

choices.text: “You lied to your best friend so she’d hate me. It worked. Look at her.”
response: “You lied to your best friend so she’d hate me,” he says. “It worked. Look at her.”
Behind him, very quietly, close to his ear: “Don’t you put me in it, fireman.”
Lena doesn’t answer. She goes quiet for longer than she has been quiet all night, long enough that he thinks he’s won something, and then she starts again on new ground, which is worse.

s09.slug: FRIDAY · 9:10 PM · I-10 EAST, THE NEW MEXICO LINE — CERTIFICATION
body: WELCOME TO NEW MEXICO comes up white in the headlights and goes by on the right, and they are in another state, and the state looks exactly like the last one: flat, black, a fence line, the far red lights of the trucks ahead.

Theo leans forward between the front seats and turns the radio on. It finds a sports station out of Tucson, still hanging on, and a man who is very sure about tendons: Freeney’s ankle, what the Colts are saying about it, what the Colts aren’t. The man has a lot of it. Margot reaches over without taking her eyes off the road and turns him off.
“I am going to be sick,” Laney says, behind Jack. “I mean it.” She doesn’t mean the road.
Kevin reaches back between the seats without turning around and holds out a plastic Safeway bag from the first-aid kit, folded square. Laney takes it and holds it in her lap with both hands.
Hale’s copy is on Jack’s knee, his hand flat on the cover. Lena looks at it in the dash light across Theo’s lap. She looks at him.

“You know what Binx calls it,” she says. “In that book. When he goes to the movies and there’s his own neighborhood up on the screen, his own street, and he walks out and all of a sudden it’s a real place to him. He’s *certified*.” She knows it cold; she doesn’t reach for a page. “That’s her, Jack. Nothing has happened to that girl until somebody’s seen it. The Walk. The singalong. The tacos. A parking lot at a quarter to five with a priest in it. Certified, every one. It isn’t real till it’s in the movie.”

“That’s backward.” He’s got the book up off his knee, and his thumb finds the corner of the print where it lies in the pages, face-down, and stays there. “Percy’s whole point is that’s the *sickness*. That’s what’s wrong with Binx. The man who has to see his street in a movie to believe he lives on it is the sick one, Broussard. That’s the joke. That’s the book.”
“I know the book.”
“Then read it.”
“I read it on the seawall at the lakefront when I was sixteen, Jack. It’s my city in it. Binx lives in Gentilly. I could walk you to his street.”
“Then you know what he does all day. He sits in the dark and watches other people be alive. That’s the sick part. Not the people on the screen. Him.”
“Exactly,” Lena says. “So who’s in the seat, Jack? Who’s sitting in the dark watching her be alive?”
It goes in. He feels it go in, and he gives her nothing on his face, and she watches him give her nothing.
She lets Percy go. She reaches for the lot.

“She hit her mark, Jack,” Lena says. “Father Osei said *stand*, and she asked him for her blocking. I heard her across the hood. And she found her light.” Her voice doesn’t go up; it goes careful, precise, a woman reading back a list. “The circle at a quarter to five. The eyes shut, the head down, beautiful. The water on the back of her hand, and she held it up and looked at it like she was checking it for her close-up. The Walk in your flannel.”

body.text: “Candlemas, with a candle. She held your candle so you could kneel there.”

body: “She’s wearing it,” Lena says. “All of it. Like wardrobe. The candle and the water and the circle, every bit of it a costume she’ll give back when she’s done with it, and you hand it to her. You *dress* her in it.” Her pen is in her fist. “You think you’re being respectful. That’s not respect. That’s blocking.”
Behind him Laney’s hands tighten on the Safeway bag. Beside him Theo’s hands come up off his knees.

“She has not pretended to believe one single thing she doesn’t,” he says, and it is louder than Tucson, louder than anything he has said tonight, loud enough that Kevin’s shoulders come up. “Not to me. Not to Osei. Not to you. She came to Mass with me and asked me after to explain it, properly, start to finish, and listened to every word of the answer. She walked the Walk and argued every sign on it fair and didn’t make fun of one. She stood because a priest asked her to stand. She shut her eyes because that’s what you do when somebody’s praying for you. That’s called *manners*, Lena. They’ve got it in Louisiana. She stood in a circle in a parking lot at a quarter to five, with a plane to catch, and let a priest bless her with water, and said *amen* to it.” He’s run out of breath and found more. “That’s more than you’ve done for her.”

“For *her*?” Lena says. “Lord have mercy. I told her safe flight. To her face, across a hood, at a quarter to five in the morning. I meant it.” She pulls the hood of her sweatshirt down off her head as if it had gotten hot in there. “I hope it was.”

“You told her safe flight across a hood,” Jack says, “with six people and a priest standing there to hear you say it. Best thing you did all week, and you did it in the light, where we could all get a good look at you being gracious. You want to talk about blocking? You hit your mark too, Lena. You just picked a better one.”
Her face goes still in the dash light. “I *meant* it.”
“I know you did,” he says. “So did she. That’s the whole argument. You can mean a thing and still do it where people can see. You did it once this week. She does it every day of her life.”

choices.text: “Percy’s on my side. Binx gets better when he quits watching. You’re the one keeping the tape.”
response: “Percy’s on my side,” he says. “Binx gets better when he quits watching. She quit. You’re the one keeping the tape.”
“Binx gets better when he gets *married*, Costigan,” Lena says. “Read to the end.”
It lands in the van like a tray dropped in a cafeteria, and then everybody pretends very hard not to have heard it fall, and Lena goes on looking at him, and he goes on looking back.

choices.text: “She does like an audience. She grew up in front of one. That isn’t the same as lying.”
response: “She likes an audience,” he says. “Okay. She grew up in front of one. That isn’t the same as lying.”

Lena is quiet long enough for a sign to go by, mileage to Lordsburg. “No,” she says. “It isn’t.” And then, harder, because he handed her that and she can see what to do with it: “It’s worse. Liars know.”

choices.text: “You’d know about wardrobe. You veil.”
response: “You’d know about wardrobe,” he says. “You veil.”

“I veil for God.” Not a half-second’s gap. “He doesn’t have a Facebook.” Her pen comes down on the legal pad in her lap. “Mine’s black lace, and I bought it with my own money, and there is not one picture of me in it anywhere on God’s earth, and there isn’t going to be.”

choices.text: “You don’t know what she came out of. Her mother —”
response: “You don’t know what she came out of,” he says. “Her mother —”

It’s right there in his mouth, the next word and the ones after it, and every one of them would win. He stops on the second word, and he hears himself stop, the way you hear a door shut somewhere in a house when you never saw it open.
“Her mother what?” Lena says.
“Nothing. It’s not mine.”
Lena looks at him for a long count across Theo, and then she goes formal on him, every vowel in its place. “Of course it isn’t,” she says, very politely, and he finds he would have taken the jam jar.

s10.slug: FRIDAY · 9:30 PM · I-10 EAST, LORDSBURG — PERFORMING
body: Lordsburg is a few lights on the right: a motel sign with two letters out, a truck stop’s tall pole sign lit yellow, a drive-in shut for the night. Up front Kevin leans across to read the gauge past Margot’s arm.
“We’re at half,” Kevin says. “Lordsburg has a —”
“There’s nowhere to stop,” Margot says.
“There’s a *sign* for it.”
“This is the Chihuahuan Desert.”

She doesn’t take the exit. The truck-stop sign comes level with them, yellow, enormous, and slides back over Kevin’s shoulder and into the dark, and Kevin watches it in the side mirror until it’s gone. Margot’s knuckles on the wheel are white.

Behind Jack, Laney reaches over in the way-back and puts her hand on Lena’s wrist. Lena takes the wrist back. Laney’s hand stays out a moment in the dark, and then it comes and takes hold of the back of Jack’s seat, by his shoulder, and grips there, and doesn’t let go of it again.
“She plays the good girl for money,” Lena says, “and the honest girl for free.”
He has been turned round in this seat since Tucson. The belt has worn a line into the side of his neck and he can’t feel it.

“Thursdays at nine she’s Cassidy,” Lena says. “The nice one. Everybody’s little sister. That’s the job, and they pay her for it, and good for her. And the rest of the week she plays the one who’s above all that, for nothing, to anybody with a phone. The Walk on a website, with question marks after it. The singalong.” She has them all lined up, the way she had the call. “She didn’t put that one up. She didn’t have to. A stranger did it for her, which is the best kind of publicity there is. And then she wrote on *your* wall. *For everybody watching at home.*”

“It’s a *job*,” he says. “She’s good at it. They don’t hand those out. My nonna watches her every Thursday night on Glenwood Avenue and prays for Cassidy by name, and she doesn’t care that it’s a part, and God doesn’t seem to mind either.”
“Your *grandmother*,” Lena says. It stops her for the length of a reflector post going by in the lights, and then she steps over it.

body.text: “You asked Kevin for the seat farthest from me,” she says. “You should’ve asked for the hood.”
“And you kissed her like nobody was in the lot. Six of us were in the lot. One of us was a *priest*.”
“And you promised her a doubloon. In front of a *priest*.”
“And you’re going to call her at the *kickoff*. Who calls at a *kickoff*?”
“And the two of you getting out of that Saab at a quarter to five like it was a *premiere*.”

body: “You were in the lot,” he says. “You had a seat for all of it. You didn’t have to watch. You watched every second, and now you want to tell me who the audience was.”
“I was standing *in* it, Jack. Across the hood from her. I could see her count.”

“You want to talk about an audience?” He doesn’t know where his hands are until he finds one of them gripping the headrest beside Theo’s ear. “You’ve had one since the Rincon. Fourteen hours of a temperature and a window and *Kevin, tell him*. That’s a two-hander, Lena. You wrote it. You cast Kevin. You’ve been doing it at me across three states for an audience of four who can’t get out of the car, and you want to talk to me about a *stage*?”
“Costigan,” Theo says, beside him.

It comes in with the road noise, part of the car. Theo has his elbows on his knees and his face in his hands, the camel coat slid off onto the floor between his shoes, and nothing is coming out of him, no pitch, no title, nothing about a picture anybody would want to make of this.

Lena doesn’t answer the stage. She goes around it. “Kenzie Rourke says you come in the side door at Mass and leave at the blessing, so nobody has to look at you. And then you stand in a circle in a parking lot next to her with a priest, so everybody can.”

“I come in the side door because it isn’t about me. She stood in that circle because Osei asked her to, and it wasn’t about her either. Neither one of those is about you, Lena. You keep walking into the middle of things that aren’t yours and reading them out loud.”
“Everything in this car is about me, Jack.” She doesn’t even raise her voice. “I’m *in* it.”

“And today,” Lena says. “A margin. For an audience of five. At a *gas station*, with the pump running. And Magdalena Broussard sat in the side door of this van with a pen in her hand and was *gracious* about it, and Magdalena is done being gracious.”

body.text: Before the next word she falters. Half a second: her breath catches on nothing, and for that half second in the dash light she looks like the girl on the porch. He sees it. It makes him angrier.
She has run out of book. Somewhere back by the state line she stopped arguing Percy with him, and what she goes to now is the girl herself.
She goes straight through it without a pause, as she came through Tucson and the canyon and the state line, and doesn’t slow down for any of it.

body: “She’s performing *again*,” Lena says, “and you’re standing there holding the book for her.”

choices.text: “Performing.”
choices.key: Past Lordsburg Lena said Skye was performing again. You took the word apart, and then you said the thing about a movie called *Jack*.
response: “*Performing*,” he says, and takes it apart in front of her, piece by piece, with the van listening. She stood up in a circle because a priest asked. She shut her eyes because somebody was praying over her. She put up a taquería so a man with a camera wouldn’t get his picture. She asked him to read to her down a phone at a gas pump because she’d been up since four and was a long way from anybody she knew. Every one a thing done for somebody else. He lays them out across the van like tools on a tailgate and she sits there and lets him and doesn’t pick up a single one.
He opens his mouth.

choices.text: “Say it again. Say *performing* again.”
choices.key: Past Lordsburg Lena said Skye was performing again. You dared her to say it again. She did, and then you said the thing about a movie called *Jack*.
response: “Say it again,” he says. “Go ahead. Say *performing* again.”
She does. She says it slowly, every syllable of it, looking straight at him across Theo’s bowed head: “Per-*form*-ing. *Again*.”
He opens his mouth.

choices.text: “Maybe she is. At least she does it where I can see it.”
choices.key: Past Lordsburg Lena said Skye was performing again. You said maybe she is — at least she does it where you can see it. Then you said the thing about a movie called *Jack*.
response: “Maybe she is,” he says. “Maybe she is. At least she does it where I can see it.”
It isn’t a concession, and he knows it while it’s still coming out of him.
“Where you can *see* it,” Lena says.
He opens his mouth.

s11.slug: FRIDAY · 9:45 PM · I-10 EAST, PAST LORDSBURG — THE LAST LINE
body: “Sorry, I forgot how private you and Julian are. When she stars in a movie called ‘Jack’ I’ll make sure you come watch the whole thing next to me so we can see your face enjoying how authentic and humble everything is.”

He turns back around to the front. The belt lets go of his neck. His hands are shaking, both of them, and he puts them on the book on his knees to stop them, and they don’t stop, so he leaves them there and lets them shake. His heart is going like he’s run up the four flights in Delgado. He has more. There’s another one right behind that one, and one behind that, lined up and ready, each one sharper than the last, and he sits there with them in his mouth and his teeth shut on them. The window beside him has his own face in it, faint, over the dark, and he looks past it at a fence line going by and doesn’t see the fence.
Behind Theo, Lena doesn’t say anything.

He can see a slice of her without turning, in the corner of the rearview mirror where it reaches the way-back. Her mouth opens. It shuts again. Nothing comes back up into it. Her hand goes up to the medal at her collar and closes on it and stays closed. A truck comes past the other way, high and lit, and in the light going over the inside of the van her face isn’t angry anymore, and he can’t tell what it is instead, and he doesn’t want to.

Laney’s hand comes off the back of his seat and goes to Lena’s arm. Lena lets it lie. Laney says her name once, low, and gets nothing back. Lena’s phone is on her knee; she turns it face-down without looking at it and leaves her hand on top.
Beside him Theo takes his face out of his hands. He looks at the back of Kevin’s seat. He doesn’t try anything; there’s nothing in the bag.

Jack takes the RAZR out of his shirt pocket and opens it low on his knee, where the light of it won’t reach anybody. No bars. New Mexico has taken them. He shuts it and keeps it in his hand. In Burnaby it’s raining, eight degrees, and she has a call time in the morning, and his flannel is hanging in a wardrobe trailer across some parking lot from wherever she is tonight.

Kevin reaches for the glovebox, where the mix rides in its sleeve, and stops with his hand on the latch, and takes the hand back. He reaches up for the map light to put it out and finds it out already, and leaves his hand up there on the switch, because there’s nothing else to do with it.
Margot drives. Both hands. Sixty-five.

It has gone cold outside. He can feel it come off the glass into his shoulder. The stars are down to the ground on every side, out here where there’s nothing to stop them, and far ahead there is one truck, two red lights, that never gets any closer.
A long way on, a sign comes up in the headlights on the right, brown and white, CONTINENTAL DIVIDE, and goes back into the dark behind them.
Nobody says anything to anybody for a hundred and fifty miles.

s12.slug: FRIDAY · 11:55 PM · EL PASO, A GAS STATION OFF I-10 — THE TOWEL
body: The canopy lays the pumps out hard and white, six islands of it, and past the last island the lot gives out into gravel and then chain-link. Beyond the chain-link, below the grade of the interstate, runs a concrete channel with an international border down the middle of it, and beyond that a whole city has been spilled across the dark in orange and run up the side of a hill. Juárez. It looks like a lamp left on in a house the size of a county.

Margot brings the Odyssey in to pump four with the front tires exactly on the paint, sets the brake, and gets out of the driver’s seat in sections. She holds her right hand in her left and examines it. “I’d like it understood that I have not unclenched since Picacho,” she says. “I was passed outside Lordsburg by a horse trailer. The horse looked at me with what I can only describe as pity.”
Somebody has taped a square of cardboard across the card reader.

body.title: Pump four
body.text: PAY INSIDE AFTER 10 PM

body: Kevin reads it aloud, as he has read aloud everything since Marisol: the speed limits, the mile markers, the warnings on the first-aid kit. “It’s five to twelve. I’ll go in. I have the clip.”
“Welcome to Texas, y’all,” Laney says from the side door, in a voice with the stuffing gone out of it. “Pay first and God bless.”
In Kevin’s quarter-zip the BlackBerry goes off with an alarm he must have set in California. The screen says CALL CLARE (TEXAS). Kevin looks at the clip, at the screen, at the clip.
“I’ll get it.”
Theo has not said a word in two hours, and the sentence comes out of him like a door that hasn’t been opened all day. He is already past the clip, with his own wallet out of his blazer.
“Four minutes,” Kevin tells the van, and heads down the lot toward the fence with the BlackBerry up, already smiling at it.

Through the store’s front glass Jack watches Theo put a question to the clerk that takes both hands. The clerk, reading glasses on a beaded chain and a SUN BOWL lanyard, answers, and Theo looks up into the ceiling tiles for the number as if it were stenciled there. He lays a ten on the counter. It is a guess; you can tell from the parking lot. The clerk looks at the bill, at pump four through the window, at the Rolex, and rings it up. Over her head, on a bracket, a TV has the Capitol dome gone soft with snow and a reporter leaning into it in a parka, the sound off.

Theo comes back across the gravel with the slip, drops it in the way-back door pocket where the receipts go, hooks the nozzle’s latch the way Kevin showed him at Picacho, and leaves the pump to it. He goes off toward the ice machine with his hands in his blazer.

Jack takes the long way round to the restrooms, along the fence, because it leads away from the van. Kevin is at the chain-link with his back to Mexico, doing his Clare voice, which is his regular voice with the volume down and every consonant polished. “I know I said Texas. This is Texas. Respectfully, it counts.” And, a few steps on: “There’s a sign out on the interstate that says WATCH FOR WATER ON ROADWAY. In the desert. Clare, I think it’s a petition.” And: “Everyone’s fine. Everyone is hydrated. That’s the report.” And, softer, as Jack passes: “It’s good. Our Lady of La Vang has been over my head since California. She’s seen things.”

Behind him, at the corner of the building: “Okay. Okay, go to sleep. Call you from Louisiana.” When Jack looks back, Kevin is still at the fence with the call long over, still holding the red key down, as if the call might otherwise come back.

In the men’s room mirror, under the buzzing tube, a pink stripe runs down the side of Jack’s neck where the seat belt has been cutting in all night. He holds his wrists under the cold tap and dries them on the Carhartt, the dispenser being empty.

Coming back along the front of the store he passes the ice machine, a white chest on legs with ICE across the lid in blue letters meant to look frosted. Theo has the lid propped on his shoulder and a drift of cold coming up over both of them. Laney stands in it in her beanie with a Styrofoam cup, her forehead almost on his lapel. Jack hears them from the corner before he has made out that they are talking.
“It was a mistake,” Theo says.
“The whole thing,” says Laney.
They see him. Theo first, then Laney, and two faces come up open for the next sentence, and there isn’t one. Behind them the machine drops its load into the bin, a long slide of it, and finishes.
“Yeah,” Jack says. He agrees with them.
“Costigan,” Theo says, and that is all there is. Jack nods to them both and goes on toward the van.

He is leaning on the side door when they come, a minute behind him and not together. Laney sits down on the sill with the pink train case from under her seat on her knees. She works the latch and takes out an orange bottle, tips one pill into her palm, and breaks it with her nail, a small clean snap, and Theo’s hand comes down over her wrist.
“It’s a prescription, Theodore.”

He takes his hand back. She swallows one half with ice water out of the cup, puts the other half in the bottle, and presses the cap down and turns it until it clicks. Then she climbs into the van with the beanie already coming down over her eyes, and Theo is left in the open door with his hand held out a little from his side, where her wrist was.

At the far edge of the lot, past the last island, there is an air pump on a concrete pad, AIR 75¢, the hose coiled on top, and Jack walks out to it. The wind comes up off the channel with diesel in it. Behind him a pump clicks off, and no one goes to the handle.
The tin is in the left pocket of the Carhartt. The Reds are in the right.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story.
