Tuesday morning I told him I think she’s the answer. He wanted a pamphlet, framed. Then he said nobody ever asked her to be that, and an answer is heavy for the person you hand it to. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no. At midnight, to the ceiling: don’t ever make me watch that again. Thursday he dressed me for the Palisades: his charcoal suit, pinned, and a half-Windsor — a commitment, like a coat. In the mirror he said I was good at it Wednesday, and that’s what he didn’t like. Friday: “You stayed.” She kept me there. “That’s love.” Saturday I tied his for the Pi Lam formal. He wanted the January call word for word. I gave it to him once. He asked if I know what I’m going to say tomorrow, if she asks. Monday: six days. Hollis was concerned; he told him I’d been detained by the Holy See. Monday night, two legal pads with Laney: a wedding seating chart, hypothetical. Tuesday he said Sigma Rho till two and left me the room. At a quarter to two he was in the lounge with Laney, Margot and Kevin: book club, *Dubliners*. He came in at twenty past two. Wednesday he pitched me New Orleans like a movie — the Saints, the money, and then, for the first time since I’ve known him, a favor. I need you there. I said no. That night I said yes, by text, from the stairs. Kevin drives the first shift. I drive West Texas. Thursday night he’d already paid my share. I made him take it back. He took a call from his mother at the edge of the lot: sandbags; they’re saying rain Friday night on the hill. At a quarter to five he hugged Skye a long time and said something only she heard. Friday night at a gas station in El Paso, by the ice machine, he and Laney said it was a mistake. The whole thing. I agreed with them. He went in and paid for the gas himself.

choices.text: *Light one.*
choices.key: In El Paso, after the fight, you smoked one under the air pump.
response: The wind off the channel gets under the flame twice. He smokes it down to the letters with his back to the canopy, and the wind takes it sideways toward Mexico.

choices.text: *Put it back.*
response: Up on the interstate a truck downshifts for the exit and goes by. He takes his hand out of the right pocket empty, and stands there till it stops wanting anything.

choices.text: *Open the tin. Count them.*

journal.title: The Reliquary
journal.text: An Altoids tin from a pea-soup restaurant in Buellton. RELIQUARY on the lid. No. 1: the Lighthouse. No. 2: Malibu, before breakfast. No. 3: the harbor — she smoked half of it first. No. 4: a clove, on the Delgado roof, at a wake. By dispensation. Do not ask. No. 5: the Ferrer Tower, in the bells. No. 6: Lucia, a motel porch, under the stars — on the back of the receipt. No. 7: Del Playa, on the widow’s walk, on the back of a HALO OR HORNS card. All Hallows — the occasion. No. 8: the east stairs, before light, the morning after All Souls. She smoked half. On the back of an All Souls card — she wrote All Souls anyway. No. 9: Campus Point, Veterans Day, on the back of the 12:10 worship aid. No. 10: the Walgreens on Mission Street, St. Nicholas Eve, half past one in the morning, out of my own pocket. ‘For the saint.’ Into her cardigan. She’ll file it. No. 11: the Point, the last night. She took it before I could light it. ‘Not here.’ She gave me the tin to keep over Christmas. Count them. Christmas Eve, in Dad’s garage after the levee, I counted: eleven. Friday night in El Paso, by the air pump, after the van: eleven.

response: The bulb over the air pump has been dead for years, by the look of the hose. Under the air pump, out of the light, he opens the tin and counts them with one finger. Eleven. He shuts it and puts it back where it lives.

choices.text: *Open the tin. Count them again.*

journal.title: The Reliquary
journal.text: An Altoids tin from a pea-soup restaurant in Buellton. RELIQUARY on the lid. No. 1: the Lighthouse. No. 2: Malibu, before breakfast. No. 3: the harbor — she smoked half of it first. No. 4: a clove, on the Delgado roof, at a wake. By dispensation. Do not ask. No. 5: the Ferrer Tower, in the bells. No. 6: Lucia, a motel porch, under the stars — on the back of the receipt. No. 7: Del Playa, on the widow’s walk, on the back of a HALO OR HORNS card. All Hallows — the occasion. No. 8: the east stairs, before light, the morning after All Souls. She smoked half. On the back of an All Souls card — she wrote All Souls anyway. No. 9: Campus Point, Veterans Day, on the back of the 12:10 worship aid. No. 10: the Walgreens on Mission Street, St. Nicholas Eve, half past one in the morning, out of my own pocket. ‘For the saint.’ Into her cardigan. She’ll file it. No. 11: the Point, the last night. She took it before I could light it. ‘Not here.’ She gave me the tin to keep over Christmas. Count them. Christmas Eve, in Dad’s garage after the levee, I counted: eleven. Friday night in El Paso, by the air pump, after the van: eleven.

response: Under the air pump he opens the tin a second time. Eleven. Still eleven. He shuts it.

s13.slug: SATURDAY · 12:15 AM · EL PASO — THE GLOVEBOX
body: The chart taped to the dash is a seating chart. It knows where everybody’s knees go, and it has nothing to say about who drives. For that there is the glovebox. Kevin is in the passenger seat with the door open and the dome light on and the glovebox down on its hinge against his shins, and he unfolds the second sheet along creases that have been in it since the Anacapa lot, and smooths it flat on his clipboard, and holds it up into the light.

body.title: The glovebox
body.text: DRIVERS. KEVIN — MARISOL → AZ LINE. THEO — AZ LINE → PICACHO (KEVIN RIDES SHOTGUN). MARGOT — PICACHO → EL PASO. JACK — EL PASO → FORT STOCKTON. NAVIGATOR — LENA. KEVIN — FORT STOCKTON → SAN ANTONIO. THEO — SAN ANTONIO → LAFAYETTE. KEVIN — LAFAYETTE → DUPRE ST. LANEY — NO. (UNANIMOUS.) · In the margin, small, in the same capitals: RESPECTFULLY — K.

body: Jack reads it from the driver’s door with the keys in his fist, still warm from Margot’s hand. His own name, and El Paso, and Fort Stockton, a place he has never heard of and is now responsible for. Down in the margin by the fold, smaller than the rest, is something that isn’t a driver.
“Respectfully what?”
Kevin folds the sheet in half along its crease. “It’s a chart,” he says. “The chart is the chart.”

In the way-back Theo is up on one elbow, with a hand on the lump under the blanket that is Laney. “Price. Price. There’s a navigator position open.” The lump does not open. From under the beanie, from a long way down: “I will end you.” The beanie goes lower.
“Kevin,” Theo says. “I’ll navigate —”
“You drive at San Antonio,” Kevin says. “Sleep. That’s medical.”
Theo opens his mouth, and looks at the folded sheet in Kevin’s hand, and shuts it. He lies back down in the corner of the way-back with his camel coat pulled up to his chin, and shuts his eyes.

Lena has been standing by the side door all this while with the legal pad against her chest. She leans in past Kevin’s shoulder and reads the sheet where he’s holding it to the light, all of it, down to the margin. She doesn’t say anything. She reaches back into the way-back, takes the slip out of the door pocket where Theo left it, and puts it under the clip with the others. She takes the road atlas out of the pocket on the back of the passenger seat, Kevin’s mother’s Rand McNally with a church bulletin marking Arizona, and gets into the passenger seat, because the sheet says LENA.

Kevin climbs into the middle row, into Jack’s chair, and gets a plastic rosary out of the pocket of his quarter-zip. Margot is already asleep across the aisle from him, sitting bolt upright with her arms crossed over her printed maps, her glasses still on.

Jack gets in behind the wheel. Margot left the seat run up to the dash, and the wheel is in his ribs and his knees are at the dash. He drops the seat back a notch at a time on its lever until he can breathe. Across the console Lena has the atlas open on her knees and her face to her window, and the dome light goes out on its own, slowly, and leaves the dash.

choices.text: *Fix the mirrors so you can see the road and nothing else.*
response: He works the little switch on his door. The left mirror comes down onto the lane. The right one swings out past her window, and she lets it, and doesn’t turn her head. The rearview he tips up with one finger until it holds the back window and the lot behind them, the canopy and the pumps, and not one face.
He takes the van out past the air pump and up the on-ramp, and the 10 takes them, and El Paso goes back over his shoulder in orange, and ahead of the headlights there isn’t anything at all.

choices.text: *A Hail Mary for the road, under your breath, the way Pop does at the on-ramp.*
response: Pop says it every time, at the bottom of the ramp onto 680 with the Silverado in second, the same speed he says grace. Jack says it at the bottom of this one, under the engine, *Hail Mary, full of grace*, straight through to the *Amen*. Whether the passenger seat hears it, he doesn’t look to see. The ramp lifts them up out of the lights and sets them down on the 10.

choices.text: “Kevin, tell the navigator —”
response: — and he stops, because Kevin is behind him in the middle row with his eyes shut and the plastic beads going through his fingers, already into the first decade, lips moving. There’s nobody to tell it to but her. She turns a page of the atlas to a map that is mostly brown and has one red line across it. He doesn’t finish.
He doesn’t finish. He puts the van in drive.

s14.slug: SATURDAY · 3:05 AM · I-10 EAST, CULBERSON COUNTY — QUARTER TANK
body: Culberson County is dark in every direction but forward. The headlights go out ahead a little way and give up, and past where they give up there is no house, no yard light, no glow over a rise where a town might be. Now and then something comes up out of the east, a knot of amber running lights that hangs on the horizon a long time before it turns into a truck, and goes by in a slam of air that rocks the van on its springs, and then the road is empty again. On the left a long black edge cuts off the bottom of the stars. Mountains. The Sierra Diablo, if the atlas on her knees has it right.

Back at Sierra Blanca the Border Patrol had the eastbound lanes funneled down under lights like a high-school ballpark’s, and an agent in a green jacket walked a flashlight down the side of the van across six faces, four of them asleep, and leaned to the window. “Y’all U.S. citizens?” “Yes, sir,” Jack said, for all six. The flashlight rested on Laney’s beanie and moved on, and the agent stepped back and waved them through.

Since then the radio has been on scan, turned down low enough that it is mostly hiss: static, and static, and a man talking fast in Spanish over an accordion, and gone, and static again, the numbers on the display turning over and over and finding nothing they want to keep.
The clock on the dash says 2:05. Kevin set it with his thumbnail at the Colorado River, and only Kevin touches it, and somewhere back in the dark the van went out of the time it’s keeping.

Jack drives. The speedometer needle sits on sixty-five, where Kevin’s card says it lives. His eyes are full of grit. His hands stopped shaking a long way back, in El Paso, and since then there has been the white line coming at him out of the dark, dash and dash and dash, and the reflectors on their posts, and the trucks, and he has not had to think about anything that wasn’t one of those.

In the passenger seat Lena is a shape with its hood up. She has her boots up on the edge of the seat and her arms around her shins and the atlas open on top of her knees, and she has been facing her window since the on-ramp. Kevin’s card is still taped to the dash at four corners, just above her knee, in the block capitals: SPEED: 65. NOT 66. OIL AT THE AZ LINE. GAS AT HALF A TANK, NOT A QUARTER. RECEIPTS TO LENA.
Six miles short of Van Horn, without turning her head from the glass, she says it.
“Quarter tank.”
Her voice is rough from not being used. He looks down. The needle on the gas gauge is sitting on the quarter mark, exactly where the card says it must never be allowed to go.

choices.text: “Van Horn’s six miles. I’ll get it.”
choices.key: At three in the morning, short of Van Horn, Lena spoke first: quarter tank. You said you’d get it.
response: “Okay.”

A green sign comes up into the headlights, VAN HORN, and then the exit. He puts the blinker on, though the road is empty both ways, and the blinker going is loud in the van, and he takes the ramp down toward the only lit thing for fifty miles.

choices.text: “Kevin’s going to have me killed.”
choices.key: At three in the morning, short of Van Horn, Lena spoke first: quarter tank. You said Kevin was going to have you killed. She said he’d want it in writing.
response: “He’ll want it in writing.”

Something comes out of his nose that is most of the way to a laugh. In the middle row Kevin, asleep, says a word that might be *gauge* and turns his face into the headrest. The exit for Van Horn comes up green in the lights, and Jack takes it, slow, and the van rolls down the ramp toward a white canopy standing out by itself on the dark.

choices.text: “I didn’t see it.”
choices.key: At three in the morning, short of Van Horn, Lena spoke first: quarter tank. You said you didn’t see it. She said she knew; you were looking at the road.
response: “I know,” she says. “You were looking at the road.”

She pulls the atlas up off her knees and holds it to the dash light, and puts a finger on a dot, and puts the atlas back. The exit comes. He takes it, and they go down the ramp into Van Horn: a canopy, and a store, and a lot of dark around both.

s15.slug: SATURDAY · 3:15 AM · VAN HORN → KENT — ANYTHING BUT THE THING
body: Under the canopy the light comes straight down, white, onto the concrete and the pumps and the two of them, and when Jack opens his door the cold comes in after him and goes for the back of his neck. It’s the high desert in February. His breath goes up in the light. The pump handle is cold enough to hurt, and the card reader takes his card on the second swipe.
Lena gets out on her side and stands with her hands up inside her sleeves, and tips her head back.

He looks up too. He has never seen this many. Youngstown had the mill glow when he was little and the sodium lights after; Marisol has the fog. Here the sky comes down to the ground on every side, and there are so many of them that he can’t find the Dipper. In Ohio the Dipper was the only one there was. Through the middle of it runs a pale smear he has only ever seen in books.
She brings her head down and goes into the store. The pump runs. Out on the interstate a truck goes by without slowing, and the sound of it goes on a long time after it’s gone.
She comes back across the concrete with two coffees in lidded cups, one in each hand, and holds one out to him without a word.
“Thanks.”
“Mm.”
The pump clicks off. He tears the receipt out of the slot, and she holds out her hand for it, and it goes under the clip of the legal pad with the others.

The light leaves nothing out. Her hood is down. Her hair is flat on the side that was against the window, and there’s a red crease across her cheek from the seam of the seat, and the mascara is gone from yesterday, and the medal has worked its way out of the neck of her sweatshirt and hangs on the front of it. She blows across the hole in the lid and drinks, holding the cup up under her chin, and the steam goes up past her face.
Back on the 10 the canopy falls away behind them and the dark comes back. The coffee is too hot to drink and he drinks it.
A billboard comes up out of nothing on the right, lit from underneath: a cartoon telescope against a sky full of yellow stars, STAR PARTY, the observatory, an exit number. It goes by.
“We just had one,” he says.
She looks at it going away in her side mirror. “Theirs has a telescope.”
“Ours had coffee.”
She drinks some of hers, and doesn’t argue.
A few miles on, out of nowhere: “Seventy point six two.”
He waits.
“Brees,” she says. “Completion percentage. This season. It’s the record. In the history of the league.”
“You’ve been holding that since Van Horn.”
“I’ve been holding that since *September*.”
“Freeney’s ankle,” he says.
“It’s fine. It’s always fine.” She drinks her coffee. “Indianapolis lies about ankles.”
“Mama says Mémère called you.”
“She did.”
“Herself?” Lena says. “Not Mama dialing?”
“Herself. At seven in the morning.”
“What did she say?”
He thinks about it. “Don’t bring nothing.”

Lena laughs. It comes up out of her loud, at the windshield, a real noise in the dark van, and in the middle row Kevin’s breathing catches and goes on. “That’s her,” she says. “That’s her exactly. It means bring something.”
“I brought a pie.”
“Then you’ll live.”
“She said your father’s been sick to his stomach since the Vikings.”

“Since the *kick*. He couldn’t watch it. He went out and stood on the porch for the overtime and heard it from the porch, the street went up, and he came back in and lay down on the floor of the front room and didn’t talk for twenty minutes. Mama put a pillow under his head.” She sets the cup in the holder. “In 1980 he wore a bag on his head to the Superdome. A Schwegmann’s bag. Mama cut the eyeholes with her sewing scissors.” And her voice drops to the bottom of her chest and goes through Breaux Bridge on its way out: “‘Lord, I wore the bag for You. One and fifteen, I wore the bag. You owe me one.’”
“He says that?”
“Every day since the Vikings. Out loud. In the pew at the eight o’clock.”
“Where are we sleeping?”

“Y’all are in the attic. All three of you.” She ticks it off on her fingers in the dash light. “There’s a box fan Daddy put in the window up there in 1994, and it doesn’t turn off. It doesn’t have an off. It has loud and louder. There’s Remy’s mattress. There’s Remy’s Tiger poster. Don’t move the poster. And Mama’s making groceries Monday, so y’all are going to get drafted.”
“What’s behind the poster?”

“Remy’s fist, the night LSU lost to somebody he won’t say.” She takes the cup back out of the holder. “And you go up and down past Mémère. She sleeps in the front room so she can see the stairs. She’s eighty-eight. She’s never missed anybody on those stairs.”

body.text: “I owe Hale three thousand words,” he says, “on whether a Browns fan can be saved. It’s an appendix.” She drinks some coffee on it. “Saved, yes,” she says. “*Cured*, no.”

body: Kent goes by on the right, a few dark buildings and a sign, and then it’s gone too, and the road runs on east under all those stars toward a town called Balmorhea that the atlas says is there.

choices.text: *Tell her what Pop said about the Pacific.*
choices.key: At three in the morning in West Texas you told Lena what your father said about the Pacific: it was big; it’s allowed.
response: He tells her about August, the turnout on Highway 1 and Pop at the guardrail with his hands in his windbreaker, and five months of Pop never once bringing it up. “And Thursday he calls me from the garage to tell me to look at the Mississippi. And then he says, I saw the Pacific. It was big. I looked at it a while.” Jack hears his father’s voice come out of his own mouth on the next part. “It’s allowed.”
She’s quiet. Then, after a while: “That’s the best thing anybody’s ever said about an ocean.” And then, practical: “Baton Rouge. The big bridge. That’s where you look at it. Don’t let Kevin talk.”

She lets her seat back a notch and turns in it toward the middle with her knees up. By Balmorhea the cup has gone slack in her hands, tipping, and he reaches across and takes it from her and puts it in the holder, and she doesn’t wake up.

choices.text: *The worst-season contest: the ’09 Browns against the ’80 Saints.*
choices.key: At three in the morning in West Texas you and Lena argued the worst season in football, the ’09 Browns against the ’80 Saints. The Saints won by losing more.
response: “Your guys won one game,” he says. “Mine won five, and it was worse.”
“How is five *worse*?”
“Because they won the last four. Now everybody in Cleveland has hope again. That’s cruelty. Your father got to put a bag on his head and be done with it.”

“Fourteen in a row,” Lena says. “*Fourteen.* They didn’t win until December, and it was the Jets, by a point. Grown men in Schwegmann’s bags. My uncle named a dog *Aints* and the dog was ashamed.” She is up on her knee in the seat now, turned toward him, the coffee going dangerously in one hand. “Your people wear dog masks to the stadium *on purpose*.”
“That’s loyalty.”
“That’s a cry for help.” She settles back. “I win. Write it down. The Saints win by losing more.”
She puts her feet up on the dash under Kevin’s card and her arms across her chest, still winning, and by Balmorhea she is asleep like that.

choices.text: *Ask her what she’ll eat first.*
choices.key: At three in the morning in West Texas you asked Lena what she’ll eat first. Mémère’s gumbo. Whatever her daddy boils. A cold Barq’s from the bottle.
response: She doesn’t have to think. “Mémère’s gumbo. Out of the pot, standing up, before anybody says grace, and she’ll hit my hand with the spoon. Then whatever Daddy’s boiling, and he’ll be boiling something, he’ll have been boiling since noon. Then a Barq’s.” She holds up a finger. “Cold. From the bottle. The can tastes like the can.”
“That’s three things.”

“You asked what first. That’s first.” She keeps going past first: a shrimp po’boy, dressed, the bread from Leidenheimer’s that has to crack when you press it, a king cake from somewhere he’s never heard of that she will not tell Laney about because Laney will want the baby. Somewhere past Balmorhea she is in the middle of the bread again, and then she isn’t, and when he looks over she’s asleep with the sentence still in her mouth.

choices.text: *Let her talk, and listen.*
choices.key: At three in the morning in West Texas you let Lena talk, and listened: the house after the water, and her father and his brothers putting it back by hand.
response: He doesn’t ask her anything. He drives, and lets the road be quiet, and she fills it.

She talks about the house. Not the water: after. Daddy and his brothers took it down to the studs, every wall, and put it back up by hand, two years of Saturdays and some weeknights under a work light on an extension cord, and she held the flashlight. She was fourteen. They found cypress under the old linoleum in the front room, and Daddy got down on his knees and wouldn’t let anybody cover it up again. Her uncles sang. One of them only knew the first verse of anything. “Daddy hung every door in that house himself,” she says. “Not one of them shuts right. He says that’s how you know who did it.”

She has turned toward him in the seat to tell it. By Balmorhea her sentences have got farther apart, and then there isn’t another one, and when he looks over she’s asleep with her cheek against the seat back, turned toward him.

s15a.slug: SATURDAY · 4:45 AM · I-10 EAST, PAST BALMORHEA — THE RIGHT ARM
s15a.music: Willie Nelson — “Blue Eyes Crying in the Rain”
body: Somewhere before Fort Stockton her head comes over the console and down onto his shoulder.

It comes all at once, with all a sleeper’s weight, and settles, and she makes a small sound in her throat and is gone again. Her temple is on the shoulder seam of the Carhartt. Her hair has come loose from the hood, and some of it has gone into his collar, and a strand of it catches on the stubble along his jaw every time the van rides over a seam in the road. Her breath comes warm through his shirt at the collarbone, and cools, and comes warm again. The medal has swung round on its chain and lies against his sleeve, and through the canvas he can feel the small hard oval of it, and the warmth it has from her.
He drives with his left hand. His right hand is on his own knee, palm up, where it was when her head came down, and he leaves it there.

Out of the static the scan comes to a station from somewhere south of the road, and this time it holds: Willie Nelson, slow, a guitar and his voice and hardly anything else, coming in thin. When the road goes down into a low place the song goes under the hiss, and when the road comes up the other side the song is still there, a little farther off.

By the next mile marker he can feel his pulse in the shoulder she’s on. A few miles later the arm has gone to pins from the elbow down, all the way into the fingertips, and he doesn’t move it. A truck comes up behind with its brights on and pulls out and goes by, and the light runs across the inside of the van, over her face and his open hand and the cup in the holder, and away up the road, and she doesn’t wake. He is warm all down that side of him and cold down the other, where the window is. Behind him there’s only breathing: Kevin with his head against the window and the rosary gone still in his lap, Margot asleep upright with her arms crossed over her maps, two shapes in the way-back.
He drives forty miles like that, at sixty-five, with his right arm still.
Short of Fort Stockton the station goes under one last time and doesn’t come up, and he leaves the hiss where it is, low, and against his collarbone her breath goes warm, and cool, and warm.

s16.slug: SATURDAY · 5:20 AM · FORT STOCKTON — THE HANDOFF
body: Fort Stockton is a canopy, a burger sign switched off for the night on a pole over the frontage road, and the sky in the east still black. He brings the van in under the lights and puts it in park.

She wakes when it stops. She sits up and takes her head back, and pushes her hair off her face with both hands, and looks out her window at the pumps. She doesn’t say anything about it. He takes his right hand off his knee and opens and shuts it until the fingers come back to him, and he doesn’t say anything about it either.
In the rearview, in the way-back, Theo’s eyes are open. Then they aren’t.
Behind Jack, Kevin comes up out of sleep in one movement, sitting straight up in the chair with one hand already at his chest for a pen he isn’t wearing. “Where are we.”
“Fort Stockton.”

Kevin leans forward between the seats to read the gauge, well up toward F now, and then holds out his hand, palm up, to the passenger seat. Lena gives him the legal pad off her knees, receipts and clip and all, without a word. He goes through the slips under the canopy light with his lips moving, Picacho, Picacho, El Paso, Van Horn, and stops on one, and holds it up to the light like an X-ray.
“Who put ten dollars of gas in this van in El Paso.”
From the way-back, with his eyes shut: “It seemed like a lot of gasoline.”
Kevin lowers the slip. He puts it back under the clip, and smooths the clip down over it, and hands the pad back to Lena, and gets out to walk around to the driver’s door.

They change places in the cold. Kevin to the wheel, moving the seat up three notches and the mirrors back to where his mother keeps them. Margot, woken enough to be furious about it, up to the passenger seat with her printed maps against her chest. Theo, eyes shut, folds himself into Margot’s old seat on the left. Jack back to his chair on the right. Lena to the way-back, with the atlas under her arm, past him at the side door, close in the cold, her breath going up white beside his.

choices.text: “Thanks for the coffee.”
response: “Mm.”
She gets a hand on the back of his chair and goes up past it into the way-back, and sits down on her side next to Laney, and puts her hood up.

choices.text: *Nothing.*
response: She goes past him up the step into the way-back. Laney, asleep, lifts the edge of the blanket for her without waking, and Lena gets in under it and pulls her hood up.

choices.text: “Navigator.”
response: A nod, from the way-back step, with the atlas under her arm.

s17.slug: SATURDAY · 7:35 AM · I-10 EAST, SONORA → JUNCTION — MARGOT’S GIDEON
body: East of Sonora the sun is coming up straight down the windshield, low and white-gold, and it lays the Edwards Plateau out ahead of the Odyssey in long blue shadows: live oaks in the draws, cedar on the rises, road cuts of pale limestone stacked like pages. In the median a doe and two yearlings are grazing with their backs to the interstate. Pickups pass the van at eighty, a dog’s head out of every second window, and Kevin holds the right lane at sixty-five with both hands on the wheel and lets Texas go around him.

He put the mix back in at first light, without announcing it, the way he took it out at Phoenix, and the Odyssey has its music again, turned low for the sleepers. Theo is one of them, folded against the left-hand window in the camel coat with his collar up around his ears.

Jack is saying the penance. He has the part he was given and no more: two by two, a walking stick, no bread, no bag, no money in the belt. At the sandals the thread runs out, as it did yesterday at the Rincon, and he goes back to *two by two* and starts over, lips going, his shoulder against the cool of the glass.

In the front seat Margot has turned the visor mirror down and cocked it at the middle row. “Costigan,” she says, finding his eyes in it. “You have been doing something with your mouth since Sonora. It is either Scripture or a stroke, and I have made allowances for both.”
“Homework,” Jack says. “From Osei. Mark, chapter six, every morning till I’m home. I’ve got about half of it by heart and nothing to check the rest against.”

Margot does not turn around. A hand comes back between the headrests holding a small green book, cloth gone to the weave at the corners. Inside the front board, over the Gideons’ printed plate, a purple ink stamp: SANTA LUCIA MOTOR COURT. Somewhere on the Big Sur coast a nightstand has a clean rectangle in its dust.
“I’m not lending you God,” Margot says. “I’m lending you a primary source.”
“That’s theft,” Kevin says.
“It’s distribution. I’m an end user.”

Jack finds the sixth chapter, the thin paper clinging to his thumb, and it isn’t quite the Mark he was given. *Take nothing for their journey, save a staff only,* it says, *no scrip, no bread, no money in their purse; but be shod with sandals; and not put on two coats.* Osei’s had a bag and a second tunic. This one has *scrip*, which he has to get from the context, and two coats. He is wearing Danny’s Carhartt over a Marisol sweatshirt, which on a strict reading is two coats. He decides to take it as a counsel of perfection, and keeps both versions.
*In what place soever ye enter into an house, there abide till ye depart from that place.* Osei’s word was *stay.* This one is *abide*, which is slower and has a rocking chair in it.

Verse thirteen ends and the page doesn’t, and he goes on reading past where he was told to stop. A prisoner named John, put away for telling a king he can’t have his brother’s wife. A birthday. A girl who dances for the table so well that the king swears to her in front of everyone to give her anything she asks, up to half his kingdom. The girl goes out and asks her mother what to ask. *And the king was exceeding sorry; yet for his oath’s sake, and for their sakes which sat with him, he would not reject her.* The head comes in on a charger. The girl gives it to her mother.
Jack shuts the book.

Somebody, in some room, has cracked the Gideon’s spine at this chapter, and when he lets go of the cover it opens again by itself on his knee. His eye does what an eye does with an open page and goes to the nearest verse. *Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.*
In the visor mirror Margot’s eyes, which he hadn’t known were on him, go back to her map. “Field note,” she says. “You read it like somebody reading a letter.”

The sun is full up now. It comes across Kevin’s shoulder and lies on the open page, and the small print goes gold, and Jack leaves the Gideon where it fell, open on his knee, while the Odyssey carries it east.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research. Took Skye’s side about the rose. Goffman, 1956. Wrote TED in her notebook and underlined it. Gave to Partners In Health and sent the rest of us there — Farmer’s Catholic, sort of. Commented ‘Front stage.’ on my status. Wednesday night in the lounge, while Laney kept it short with Theo: keeping score. A page in her notebook says SKYE. Thursday at the Anchor she interviewed Skye for her column. She hated that it was good. Her column ran Thursday: ‘Front Stage.’ It’s good. I told her twice. Thursday she brought Salinger’s death to the window table like a lab result. Friday in the Fishbowl she took Skye on about the fundraiser: a room raised for a cause, handed to its opposition. Skye said she didn’t hand them the room, she introduced them to me, and she’s still voting for Boxer. Margot gave her one point and kept one. Four versions of Wednesday are going around Delgado, she says. Commented *Back region. Finally.* on the taco picture. Monday night in the Fishbowl: six versions of Wednesday now. One has reached the Classics department. She wouldn’t read me any of them. Thursday night at the van she took the pie on her lap, for science, and told the van about men in some societies who may not speak to their mothers-in-law; everything goes through a third party. Radcliffe-Brown. Then she turned her recorder off. Friday it was eight versions of Wednesday. Then she drove Picacho to El Paso and wouldn’t stop for anything: there’s nowhere to stop, it’s the Chihuahuan Desert. Saturday at sunup she lent me a Gideon from the Santa Lucia Motor Court. Not God. A primary source.

s18.slug: SATURDAY · 9:55 AM · SAN ANTONIO, A TRUCK STOP ON THE EAST SIDE
body: The truck stop on the east side of San Antonio sells breakfast tacos from a steel window beside the lottery machine, foil-wrapped and hot enough to hurt: potato and egg, chorizo and egg, bean and cheese, a plastic thimble of green salsa with each. Over the register a TV has the weather on, the upper right corner of the country gone white. It is cool and bright out, and the men at the counter are in work shirts with the sleeves pushed up.

They eat at a picnic table bolted to the concrete beside the ice cage, five of them in the clothes they slept in. Kevin is in a quarter-zip that has become a position. Margot is rumpled for the first time in Jack’s experience and has somehow kept every crease in place. Theo has the camel coat. Laney is awake. She has the seat-belt crease down one cheek like a sash and a taco in each hand, and she addresses the table. “My mouth tastes like Oklahoma. I’m not taking questions, comments or eye contact until the second one.”

Theo’s phone goes off on the steel between the salsa and Margot’s maps, a buzz you can feel in the bench. He reads the name on the screen. Theo, who has never in Jack’s sight left a plate unfinished, leaves a bean-and-cheese in its foil. “Excuse me. My mother. Somebody say a prayer, Costigan, it ought to be you.” It’s a good line, and it lands half a tone high. He is on his feet with the phone at his ear before the second buzz, walking, not to the restroom and not to the van but out across the lot between a Peterbilt and a stock trailer, to the far edge, where the pavement gives out into winter grass and a drainage ditch. He turns his back on the picnic table and stops.

The Odyssey sits across the lot at the diesel island with its hatch to them and its side door open. Somebody has gone over the 2 on the back glass with a sleeve and made it a 1 and left the S: WHO DAT · 1 DAYS.
At the van, Lena is trying to refold a map that has never in its life been refolded by anyone.

choices.text: Go after Theo.
Go to the van.

s18t.slug: SATURDAY · 10:00 AM · SAN ANTONIO, THE EDGE OF THE LOT — THE HILL
body: It is a hundred yards to the end of the lot, down a lane of idling reefers, each holding its own diesel note, with grackles lined along the chain-link above them working through every noise they own. Jack hears Theo before he reaches him because Theo isn’t using his phone voice. The phone voice is low and amused and closing on a yacht. This one is high and quick and has no adjectives in it.
He stops by a stack of pallets twenty feet back, where the grass starts. Theo’s camel coat is open in the sun, and his shoulders are up around his ears.

“The hill came down *when*? Before it was *light*? In the *street*. What do you mean, in the — cars? In the storm drains?” A pause. “Who told you to — a *deputy*. Okay. And the barriers, the concrete ones, where are the —” A longer pause. “They *moved?*”
“Mom. Is the house — okay. Okay. And the — no. *Don’t.* Don’t go in it. Let them — Mom. Leave it.”

His free hand comes up and drags down his face from the forehead and stays over his mouth. “Is Poppy with you. Good. Poppy does not get to go back for her shoes. Tell her I said, and tell her I said it nicely.” He listens a long time. “Where are you.” Another silence, shorter. “Bunny’s. In Pasadena. Good. Bunny’s is on a flat. Stay at Bunny’s, stay *there*. I’ll call you tonight. Yes. Okay.”

He takes the phone from his ear and looks at it and presses the button, and stands with it hanging at his side while a reefer cycles on behind him and goes quiet. A trucker at the next trailer is eating a taco off a pocketknife and not looking at anything. Then Theo turns, and his face is already on: the half smile, the weight on one hip, the eyebrows up for business. It takes him a second to find Jack at the pallets, and it doesn’t slip.

“Costigan. You look like a telegram. There isn’t any news.” He puts the phone away in the coat. “My mother’s pool is now a pond. She’s taking it very well. She’s at the Huntington with a Bloody Mary and the dogs.”

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story. Tuesday morning I told him I think she’s the answer. He wanted a pamphlet, framed. Then he said nobody ever asked her to be that, and an answer is heavy for the person you hand it to. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no. At midnight, to the ceiling: don’t ever make me watch that again. Thursday he dressed me for the Palisades: his charcoal suit, pinned, and a half-Windsor — a commitment, like a coat. In the mirror he said I was good at it Wednesday, and that’s what he didn’t like. Friday: “You stayed.” She kept me there. “That’s love.” Saturday I tied his for the Pi Lam formal. He wanted the January call word for word. I gave it to him once. He asked if I know what I’m going to say tomorrow, if she asks. Monday: six days. Hollis was concerned; he told him I’d been detained by the Holy See. Monday night, two legal pads with Laney: a wedding seating chart, hypothetical. Tuesday he said Sigma Rho till two and left me the room. At a quarter to two he was in the lounge with Laney, Margot and Kevin: book club, *Dubliners*. He came in at twenty past two. Wednesday he pitched me New Orleans like a movie — the Saints, the money, and then, for the first time since I’ve known him, a favor. I need you there. I said no. That night I said yes, by text, from the stairs. Kevin drives the first shift. I drive West Texas. Thursday night he’d already paid my share. I made him take it back. He took a call from his mother at the edge of the lot: sandbags; they’re saying rain Friday night on the hill. At a quarter to five he hugged Skye a long time and said something only she heard. Friday night at a gas station in El Paso, by the ice machine, he and Laney said it was a mistake. The whole thing. I agreed with them. He went in and paid for the gas himself. Saturday in San Antonio his mother called from a friend’s house in Pasadena: the hill came down in the night. Her pool’s a pond. He told her to leave it. He says she’s at the Huntington with a Bloody Mary and the dogs.

choices.text: “Do you need to go home?”
choices.key: In San Antonio Theo’s mother called: the hill came down in the night. You asked if he needed to go home. He said he needs to be in New Orleans.
response: Theo’s mouth is already open on the next thing; Jack can see the shape of it, something with a swizzle stick in it. It closes.
“No,” he says. “I need to be in New Orleans.”
His eyes go to the ditch and come back. He claps Jack on the arm, hard, and they start back across the lot, Theo a half step ahead, the camel coat flapping.

choices.text: “A pond. Lena’s dad will want to stock it.”
choices.key: In San Antonio Theo’s mother called: the hill came down in the night. You told him Lena’s father would want to stock the pond. He laughed.
response: Theo’s head goes back and a bark of laughter comes out of him that he plainly hadn’t arranged. “Redfish,” he says. “He’d want redfish. He’d put in a crab trap and call it a water feature.” He wipes an eye with the heel of his hand and blames the sun. “Tell Tony I’m taking bids.”
They start back across the lot, Theo laughing again at the Peterbilt for no reason it has given him.

choices.text: “That’s twice you’ve told her not to go in the pool house.”
choices.key: In San Antonio Theo’s mother called: the hill came down in the night. You said that was twice he’d told her not to go in. It’s full of mud, he said.
response: Theo smiles at him. It’s a good smile; it has all its teeth.
“It’s full of mud, Costigan,” he says, still smiling. “I don’t want my mother in mud.”
They start back across the lot.

s18v.slug: SATURDAY · 10:00 AM · SAN ANTONIO, THE VAN — DAYLIGHT
body: Out at the van the sun has some warmth in it for the first time today. It comes low and yellow across the truck lot, off the windshields of the rigs idling in their rows, and it shows up every crumb on the Odyssey’s floor mats and the haze on the inside of the glass where six people have been breathing since Marisol.

Laney is in the way-back with the hatch up, flat on her back across the bench, her boots out over the bumper and her sunglasses pushed up into her hair. A breakfast taco in its foil rides on her chest, unopened, going up and down. She hasn’t said a word since the taco counter, and her face would like it known that she intends to keep it that way.

Lena is standing in the open side door with a map of Texas. It’s the big free highway map, and at some point this morning somebody opened it to its full size, and it doesn’t want to go back. She has the Gulf folded under. She has El Paso folded under. In the middle the rest of the state bellies up out of her hands, and there’s a brown coffee ring on the Hill Country where she must have set her cup down on it.

Jack comes across from the restaurant with the last of his coffee and stops, because she’s in the door and his chair is behind her. In the daylight she looks like the night she’s had: the dark under her eyes, the sweatshirt she slept in, her hair twisted up off her neck and held there by a pencil stuck through the knot.
She looks up at him over Texas and holds out a corner of it.
“Can you hold this end.”

He sets the coffee on the roof of the van and takes the end. She folds her side toward him along a crease that’s printed right there, and he folds his side toward her along a crease that’s printed right there, and they turn out to be different creases, and Texas comes up in a peak in the middle with San Antonio on top.
“No,” Lena says.

They open it back out and do it again, slower, her way, with her telling him when. It goes wrong in a new place. The legend ends up on the inside. The cover ends up somewhere in the Panhandle, upside down.
She takes the map out of his hands in one wad and crams it into the pocket of the sliding door, on top of the legal pad, and leans on it with the heel of her hand until it stays.
“It lives there now.”

Hale’s *Moviegoer* is on the seat of his chair just inside the door, where he left it to go in for tacos: the cover curling, the spine gone white in its creases, the pages fat from some bath a long time ago. She sees it. She doesn’t pick it up.
“That’s not yours.”
“Hale’s. He lent it to me.”
She reads the cover upside down, the way it’s lying, with her hands in the pouch of her sweatshirt.
“Is it any good?” she says. “His?”

choices.text: “Yours is better.”
choices.key: In San Antonio Lena asked if Hale’s copy is any good. You told her hers is better.
response: She looks up off the book at him, straight, in the full sun. He means the margins. Her mouth comes open on something and shuts on it again, and she reaches up and pushes the pencil deeper into the knot of her hair, and leaves it at that.

choices.text: “He wrote *Quite not* next to a sunset.”
choices.key: In San Antonio Lena asked if Hale’s copy is any good. You told her Hale wrote *Quite not* next to a sunset. Hers is better, she said. You said yeah.
response: “That’s very Hale.” She tips her head to read the spine the right way up. And then, on her own: “Mine’s better.”
“Yeah.”
She nods, as if that’s settled a thing that needed settling, and pushes the door pocket shut on the map with her knee.

choices.text: “I’ve got yours at home. I read it twice.”
choices.key: In San Antonio Lena asked if Hale’s copy is any good. You told her you’ve got hers at home, and you’ve read it twice.
response: She doesn’t answer that. She pulls the map back out of the door pocket and opens one panel of it and closes it again, and opens another, though there’s nothing left in it that folding is going to fix. The tops of her ears have gone red.

s19.slug: SATURDAY · 5:45 PM · I-10 EAST, THE ATCHAFALAYA BASIN BRIDGE — DUSK

body.text: Theo comes back across the lot with his phone in his pocket and his face arranged, and Laney, watching Lena watch Jack, puts her sunglasses back on.
body.else: Theo walks back to the van beside him with his phone in his pocket and his face arranged.

body: Theo drives. Houston takes two hours out of the middle of the day, freeways stacked on freeways and the same skyline turning up in a different window every time Jack looks for it. Beaumont. A long rise over a river going brown into the marsh, and a blue sign at the top: WELCOME TO LOUISIANA, and under it, smaller, *Bienvenue en Louisiane*. In the way-back Lena sits up to read it. Then Lake Charles, and the tall bridge there, and the flat country after it.

At Lafayette there’s a gas station with boudin turning under a heat lamp by the register. Kevin buys a link for everybody on principle and reads the ingredients aloud to anyone who will stand still — “Pork, rice, liver. It’s a casserole in a casing. I love it.” — and takes the keys back. Theo gets in up front. Lena comes out of the restroom last and gets in on the right side of the way-back, directly behind Jack, and pulls her belt across, and nobody says a word about it.

body.text: “Your seat,” she says, behind him. “Put it up.” He puts it up. It’s the first thing she has said to him since Fort Stockton, and she says it to him, not to Kevin.

body: East of town the land gets low and wet, and then it quits. The interstate goes up onto concrete legs and stays up, two spans running side by side out over the water for eighteen miles, and the water is everywhere: black, flat, standing among cypress that come up out of it with their knees showing and moss hanging off their arms in gray rags. The sun is low behind them. It lays the van’s shadow out long on the bridge ahead and turns the tops of the trees to copper while the water underneath goes dark first.

Theo has found a station at the bottom of the dial out of Lafayette. When he found it a man was talking French between records, easy, a neighbor over a fence. Now it’s an accordion, pumping, with a rubboard rattling along under it, and a man singing in a French that Jack knows from menus, and none of this is on one.

Lena has been awake since Lafayette. Somewhere at the start of the bridge she comes forward out of the way-back with her belt let out to the end of its strap, and folds her forearms on the top of his seat. He feels her lean come through the seatback into his shoulders. Her arm goes past his face to point.
“Heron.”
A big gray one, on one leg in the shallows at the edge of the trees, lifts off as they come level with it and goes away low over the water with its legs hanging.

“That’s a man running his traps.” Out where the cypress thins, an aluminum skiff is working down a line of floats, and a man in the bow is hauling something up dripping. “See his boots?” White rubber, to the knee. “Cajun Reeboks.”
“Is that what they’re called?”

“That’s what they’re called by everybody who doesn’t have to wear them.” Her sleeve goes across his cheek as she swings her arm around to point back past his shoulder, into the light, the way they came. “Mémère’s people are back that way. Breaux Bridge. Her daddy fished all this before there was a bridge to fish it from.”
Jack looks wherever she points — the heron, the skiff, the low sun — and keeps his head where it is. Her face is just behind his shoulder. He knows exactly where, and he looks at the water.
At the wheel Kevin’s eyes go up to the rearview and come back down to the road.
“Huh,” Kevin says, very quietly.
Beside Jack, Margot has her notebook open on top of her printed maps. She writes, and reads it off as she goes. “The avoidance relationship has been suspended. Cause unknown.”
“Margot,” says Laney, from the way-back.

Up front Theo pulls his visor down, though the sun is behind them, and slides open the little mirror on the back of it. In that square of glass he and Laney find each other, and both look away fast: two people who have seen a ghost and would rather not scare it off.

Lena is still leaning on his seat. The accordion goes on, and under it, close at his ear and low enough to be his alone: “I asked Kevin for the way-back so I wouldn’t have to look at you for thirty hours.”
The bridge lifts over a channel where a barge is tied up dark against the trees, and comes back down.
“Turns out the way-back’s where you see the back of everybody’s head.”

choices.text: “What’s he singing?”
response: “*Bon ton roulet.*” She listens to the next bit. “Let the good times roll. Roughly.” And she keeps going, a line behind the singer, translating with total confidence, and it turns out the song is about a man who drove thirty-five hours in somebody’s mother’s minivan for one plate of crawfish, and would do it again, and his friends were no help to him at all.
“That’s not what he’s singing.”
“No. I made it up.” She settles her chin on her forearms. “It’s what he means, though.”
The bridge runs out of water and into trees, and behind them the dark comes down over the Basin fast, the copper gone off the cypress, the water and the sky gone the same black.

choices.text: “We’re going to be thirty-five hours. Theo said thirty.”
response: Theo flips his visor back up. “I said *approximately*.”
Behind Jack’s seat Lena laughs, short, into her own sleeve.
“Approximately is a range, Costigan. Thirty is in it. Thirty-five is in it. Technically, so is forty. I was very careful.”
The bridge comes down off its legs into trees, and Kevin reaches for the headlights.

choices.text: “I know. I could feel it.”
response: Her forearms come off his seat. She sits back, and behind him there’s no sound at all for the rest of the record, not even her belt. When the man comes back on talking French, her knuckle knocks against the back of his headrest, one soft knock, and nothing after it.
The van comes off the end of the bridge into trees, and he can still feel the knock at the back of his head.

s20.slug: SATURDAY · 7:50 PM · N. DUPRE STREET, MID-CITY — THE STEPS
body: Lena is asleep before Baton Rouge. Somewhere past the end of the Basin the weight goes off the back of Jack’s seat, and when he turns his head she is folded into the corner of the way-back against her window, directly behind him, her cheek on her own sleeve and her mouth a little open.

At Baton Rouge the interstate climbs a long steel bridge, and the Mississippi goes under them in the dark. It is wider than he had it in his head, black and moving, with lights on it: a towboat shoving a raft of barges upstream under one white lamp, the refineries strung out along the far bank, red lights blinking on the stacks. The water takes the lights and pulls them long downstream. Jack looks at it for the length of the bridge, and then twisted round in his chair, out the back glass past Lena asleep, until the levee closes over it.

After that an hour of dark, swamp on both sides of a road up on legs; the airport; New Orleans coming up on the right in a long low spill of orange; and Kevin at the wheel reading exits off Margot’s printout under his breath and taking the one for Carrollton.

N. Dupre Street is narrow and dark under its oaks, the sidewalks heaved into slabs by the roots, cars parked half up on the curb the length of the block. Half the porches are hung with black and gold. Somebody has painted a fleur-de-lis on a garbage can. The Broussards’ house sits up on piers at the top of a flight of wooden steps, long and narrow and running straight back from the street, the porch light on and the front door open behind the screen. In the side yard, under a work light clamped to the corner of a shed, a propane burner is going with a sound like a jet that has decided to stay, and the steam off a pot the size of an oil drum goes up white through the light and into the branches. Back there somewhere a radio: WWL, a man and a woman talking over each other about precincts, and the polls about to close.
Kevin brings the Odyssey in against the curb behind a pickup with WHO DAT soaped across its back glass, puts it in park, sets the brake and turns off the engine. In the quiet the burner roars.
“Thirty-five hours and forty minutes,” Kevin says. “Theo.”

body.text: “Within tolerances,” says Theo, already out his door.
body.else: “Approximately,” says Theo, already out his door.

body: The doors come open on both sides and the night comes in, cool and damp, boiling spice off the yard and a sweetness on the air from somebody’s bush that Jack doesn’t have a name for. Margot gets out holding her maps. Laney climbs over the bench from the way-back, stiff in every joint, and stops with one boot on the step to look down at Lena, who hasn’t moved.
“She sleeps like she’s being paid for it,” Laney says.

Jack gets her out without deciding to. He has her duffel up off the floor and over his shoulder, and then he is in between the chairs on one knee with an arm under her knees and the other behind her back, and she comes up off the bench all at once, warm from sleep and heavier than she looks, and her head drops into the hollow under his collarbone and settles. Her hair has come half out of its knot, and it falls over his arm. She says something into his shirt that isn’t a word. He backs out of the van with her, and on the sidewalk the others stand with their bags and let him by.

The steps go up a full story to the porch, steeper than steps have any business being, built by somebody who expected water. He takes them one at a time with her weight against his chest and the duffel knocking at his hip. Somewhere around the middle the pencil works loose, and he hears it go down them behind him, step by step, into the dark. In her sleep her hand has found a fistful of his shirt front, and it doesn’t let go.

Her mother is in the door. Jack has never laid eyes on her and would know her anywhere: Lena’s chin and Lena’s eyes, thirty years on and tired, in blue scrubs with a cardigan over them and one hand holding the screen door wide. She watches him come up her stairs with her daughter. The screen door doesn’t move in her hand, and she doesn’t ask him one thing.
“Second door on the left, baby,” she whispers, and stands back to let them in.

The hall runs straight back through the house, room opening off room, every light on, the smell of the boil coming down it from the yard. The second door on the left is a narrow room with a twin bed under a crucifix and a Saints pennant from 1987, the felt gone soft as a dish towel. Somebody has turned the bed down. He lays her on it, and she turns her face into the pillow and is gone again.
“Boots,” Celeste whispers from the doorway.
He works her Justins off, heel and toe, and sets them side by side under the bed, and puts the duffel at the foot of it, and backs out of the room past her mother.

Out on the porch the others have come up with the bags and are standing in a row by the swing, Margot with Gloria’s white box held upright in both hands. In the swing sits a small old woman in a housedress and a gray cardigan, with the tail of a rosary hanging out of the cardigan pocket and her feet not quite reaching the boards.

body.text: “*Le garçon de l’Ohio.*” It is a voice he knows from three phone calls, and it comes out of a much smaller person than he had built for it.

“You came to my house first.”
“You said yes. Now you’re here.”

body: “Yes, ma’am.”
Theo steps up beside him with his overnight bag on his shoulder and the smile he keeps for other people’s mothers. “Madame Broussard. Theo Vance. I’ve taken the liberty of a suite at the Roosevelt —”
“You sleep here.”
“Yes, ma’am.”
Behind him Laney mouths *I told you* at the back of his head.

Mémère puts one foot down and stops the swing. “Boys in the attic. Girls downstairs, with Magdalena and them. And me, I sleep in the front room.” She tips her head at the window behind her, where a lamp is lit beside a made-up daybed. “Where I can see the stairs.”
Going back down for Kevin’s cooler, Jack finds Lena’s pencil on the third step from the bottom and puts it in his shirt pocket.
Inside, at the foot of the attic stairs, Celeste stops him with a hand on his sleeve. She keeps her voice at a whisper that carries exactly as far as he is.
“She doesn’t sleep in cars,” she says. “Since she was little. She’d stay up all the way to Lafayette.”

journal.title: Celeste Broussard
journal.text: Lena’s mother. A nurse — she came to the door in scrubs. Gives her orders in a whisper. Saturday night she was in the door when I came up her steps with Lena asleep, and she didn’t ask me one thing.

journal.title: Odile Broussard (Mémère)
journal.text: Lena’s Mémère. Breaux Bridge. Eighty-eight. The monks’ fruitcake came; it’s *trop sec*; she’s eating it anyway. Prayed for Wes at the eight o’clock. *Quelqu’un devait demander.* Asked for le garçon de l’Ohio. Wes told her I’m skinny. I said oui, madame. She says I have manners. The Friday before I flew back she took the phone for ten seconds to ask was I eating. When I come to New Orleans I come to her house first. Thursday at seven in the morning she called me herself, from Dupre Street, on a number the redhead gave her. She knew I’d said yes. She called anyway: I don’t come because the rich boy asked me, I come because she asked me. Don’t bring nothing. Come to this house first — I said it back to her. Lena told her not to call. Saturday night on the porch she cancelled Theo’s hotel. You sleep here. Boys in the attic. She sleeps in the front room, where she can see the stairs.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes. Thursday at the window table he had a list: things to say at hour four. He’d heard about Hale’s — Laney to Margot to him — and didn’t take a side. Then he asked me what you’re supposed to feel at hour four. I told him. He wrote it down. Clare asked him which of us was right at Hale’s; he told her he didn’t have the information, and she said that was a very Kevin answer. He asked if my brother’s okay. Thursday night at the van he had a clipboard and a seating chart taped to the dash, and said he’s pre-med, not a switchboard. Clare came to see him off. At three in the morning he was at St. Brendan’s ahead of me. Couldn’t sleep either. At a quarter to five Osei blessed his mother’s car again. Still pretty blessed. Friday under the dinosaurs at Cabazon he told Theo and Laney to leave it alone. He checked the oil at the Arizona line. He called Clare from El Paso, like he said he would. He kept the clock the whole way: thirty-five hours and forty minutes.
