s21.slug: SATURDAY · 8:05 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE SIDE YARD — THE BOIL
body: In the side yard the work light makes a room out of the dark: the low arm of the oak overhead, the board wall of the shed, a picnic table, a cooler, a folding lawn chair with a cushion on it, and in the middle of it the burner, roaring blue under the pot. Over the pot stands Tony Broussard with a paddle the size of an oar. He is somewhere in his fifties and big, gone soft in the middle and hard everywhere else, in a BROUSSARD’S SEAFOOD · BANKS ST. T-shirt under an open flannel, with steam in his eyebrows. A mesh sack of crawfish slumps against the cooler, alive and rustling, small and dear this early in the season, and in the red water corn and new potatoes and garlic by the head go round and round.
He sees Jack and leans the paddle on the rim and comes around the pot with his hand out. It is a fish market’s hand, wet and enormous, and he looks Jack over while he shakes.
“The Ohio boy.”
“Yes, sir. Jack.”
“Browns?”
“Yes, sir.”
Tony shuts his eyes. “Lord, son.” He opens them again on the van at the curb. “How long that took y’all?”
“Thirty-five hours and forty minutes, sir,” says Kevin, coming through the side gate with an armful of sleeping bags.
“Thirty-five *hours*? In a *Honda*?”
“It’s an Odyssey, sir,” Kevin says. “It’s a very good car.”

Tony looks at Kevin, and at the van, and back at Kevin, and goes back to his paddle, stirring from the bottom with his back in it. “You hear what the league did to us? Sent lawyers. *Lawyers.* To T-shirt men. A man on Decatur with a card table and his kids’ tuition in a cigar box, and they send him a letter says *Who Dat* is theirs.” He knocks the paddle on the side of the pot. “So the senator writes them a letter back, and the attorney general got in it, and they quit. Course they quit. You can’t own what a city hollers. Who’s it belong to, the man selling the shirt, or the man in section whatever since nineteen eighty-one? And before that with a bag on his head.”

Ten minutes after that the paddle is in Jack’s hands, and he couldn’t say how. Tony said, “Here, hold this,” and went in the shed for the corn, and came back with the corn and without any interest in the paddle. “From the bottom,” he says, over Jack’s shoulder. “Like you mean it.” He reaches past him and punches the radio off in the middle of a woman saying *turnout* and puts a tape in the boombox on the shed’s windowsill, and a piano comes rolling out of it, slow and easy, and a voice like gravel in cane syrup. “Enough of that. They can call it without me.”
After that the family comes in waves, out the back door and down the back steps into the light, and every one of them already knows who he is.

Remy first — the LSU cap on backward tells Jack which one before anybody does — with a beer in his hand, who grabs Jack’s free hand over the paddle and pumps it. “Brother-in-law!” He is very pleased with this. Tony doesn’t tell him to stop.

Luc comes after him, the oldest, off duty, compact in a Saints sweatshirt and a haircut that says cop from across the yard, who shakes his hand once and says, “Luc,” and takes up a place against the fence with a can of Barq’s. From there he can see the gate, the pot, the back door, and Jack. He watches all four.

Tess is next, with Beau behind her carrying a diaper bag and a folding chair, and in the crook of her arm a bundle in a black-and-gold knit cap, seven weeks old and asleep through all of it. Tess looks at Jack over her daughter’s head with frank interest, a woman sizing up help.

The twins come at a run, thirteen, in Saints shirts down to their knees. Josie stops dead in front of the pot. She has Lena’s eyebrows and Lena’s way of standing with her weight on one hip, ready for a fight.
“Are you the Ohio boy?”
“Yes.”
“You’re not the violin.”
“No.”
“*Good.*”
She walks off. Jude doesn’t say anything. He steals a potato out of the colander on his way past and eats it hot, blowing on his fingers.

When Celeste comes out on the back steps, changed out of her scrubs, Laney is at the bottom of them. Celeste stops two steps up and looks at her: the copper hair, the quilted vest, the face that has been shut all day.
“So *you’re* my redhead.”

And Laney Price, who has called this woman every night for a week, bursts into tears. Celeste comes down the last two steps and gathers her in, and Laney cries into the front of her cardigan for no reason she gives anybody, and Celeste rubs her back in small slow circles between the shoulder blades, a nurse’s circles, and says, “I know, baby. I know,” over the top of her head.

Margot has been given the corn, a step stool and a garbage bag for the husks, and shucks with her sleeves shoved up to the elbow, ruthless and quick, looking happier than Jack has seen her since Big Sur. Kevin has been fed twice: once by Celeste, a bowl of something from the stove inside, and once by Mémère, who did not see the first bowl and would not have believed in it. Mémère herself has been installed in the lawn chair with a jelly glass. Theo is down on one knee beside it, charming her. She lets him finish, and says something in French to the twins, and the twins fall about. Theo regroups and charms her again, slower, and this time at the end of it she hands him her glass to hold while she gets her rosary untangled from her pocket. He fails better.
Tony is at Jack’s elbow with a jelly glass of his own, amber, a curl of lemon peel riding in it and the smell of licorice coming off it from a foot away. He holds it out to him across the burner.
“Sazerac. I make them myself. Rye whiskey, Peychaud’s, a little sugar, the Herbsaint just to wet the glass.” The glass hangs there in the steam. “You drink, son?”

journal.title: Tony Broussard
journal.text: Lena’s father. Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Twenty-eight years in the same seats. Held the phone up to the kitchen radio for the whole second half while we lost him at every curve on Highway 1. Wes told him there’s a Browns fan out here. Laney had him at hello. Saturday night in the side yard he put me on the paddle inside ten minutes.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’ At Sully’s Skye brought her a present. She wore her own bells. She gave Skye advice, and I told her I’ve seen her work. Then she took a shot at Skye, and Skye was handling it, and I didn’t let her. I’ve never yelled at Laney before. The whole bar heard. Tuesday, after the storm, she came back down to the laundry room by herself, with a list: the airport, the status, Sully’s, the jacket, me. She asked what I’m doing. I told her the truth, which I haven’t told anybody. Then I left her standing there. I’m done with that room. Both of them. Friday on the west stairs she and Theo were doing a bit at each other about memory. I said morning. In the lounge she died across the arm of the couch over a picture of tacos. Then she looked at me a long time. Monday night she and Theo were on the lounge floor with two legal pads side by side, and turned them over when I came in. A wedding seating chart, Theo said. Hypothetical. She took ink off my face with her thumb, and went cold again. Thursday night at the van she said she wasn’t Western Union and relayed everything anyway. She packed me a bag: FIREMAN, LARGE. Thirty hours. Behave. She told me Julian isn’t coming, like I’d care, and I told her so. Friday night in El Paso she broke a pill in half with her nail. It’s a prescription, Theodore. Saturday on Dupre Street Lena’s mother said So you’re my redhead, and Laney cried in her arms and didn’t say why.

choices.text: “Abita, sir, if it’s the same to you.”
choices.key: In the side yard Tony put you on the paddle and held out a Sazerac. You asked for an Abita. He let you.
response: “It’s not the same to me,” Tony says. “But you’re company.” He drinks the Sazerac himself in two swallows, digs an Abita out of the ice, knocks the cap off on the edge of the picnic table and puts the cold bottle in Jack’s free hand.

He takes the paddle back. He looks into the pot, and at the sky, and at his watch, and turns around to his yard and his family and half of Dupre Street, and his voice goes up over the piano and the burner both: “*Dump it!*”

choices.text: *Drink the Sazerac.*
choices.key: In the side yard Tony put you on the paddle and held out a Sazerac. You drank it. It was very strong.
response: It is very strong. It goes down like a lit match and keeps going, rye and licorice and sugar, and the back of his throat shuts and his eyes run, and Remy, overjoyed, pounds him on the back.

Tony watches him get it down, satisfied about something, and takes back the paddle. Jack is still holding the jelly glass with a finger of it left in the bottom when Tony turns to the yard, fills his chest, and roars: “*Dump it!*”

choices.text: “Whatever Mémère’s drinking, sir.”
choices.key: In the side yard Tony put you on the paddle. You said you’d have whatever Mémère was drinking. Mémère was drinking a Sazerac.
response: Mémère is drinking a Sazerac. It is very strong. Tony is so pleased he has to set the paddle down; he gives Jack his own glass and pours himself another out of a pitcher on the cooler, and across the yard Mémère lifts hers at Jack from the lawn chair, and Jack lifts his back, and drinks, and the edges of the yard go soft.
Tony cups both hands round his mouth and turns toward the back steps: “*Dump it!*”

s21a.slug: SATURDAY · 8:45 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE TABLE — THE SEAT
body: Tony and Luc lift the basket out of the pot between them, streaming, and walk it to the long table Beau and Remy have made out of two sawhorses and a door under the work light, laid with three thicknesses of the *Times-Picayune*, and upend it down the middle: a red landslide of crawfish, corn, potatoes split by the heat, garlic gone soft in its skins, and a few blue crabs from the market boiled orange. The steam goes up into the light. For a second everybody stands and looks at it, and then everybody sits.

Celeste points Jack into a chair halfway down the far side — “There, baby” — and goes for paper towels. Margot has the chair on one side of him. On the other side the bench at the end of the table is empty.

He has been in the chair about a minute when Tess comes round behind him and puts her daughter in his arms. “Hold her for me, I need a hand,” she says, and takes the hand back to her own place and uses it to eat, and doesn’t come back for the baby. Lucille weighs about what a sack of flour does and is a great deal warmer. She sleeps in her black-and-gold cap with one fist up by her face, and when he shifts her into the crook of his left arm she opens her mouth and thinks about crying and doesn’t.

Margot has kept Gloria’s white box out of the twins’ reach all evening, on top of the refrigerator, and now she brings it out and sets it down on the newspaper in front of him, since it’s his to answer for.

body.text: Mémère sees it from the head of the table: the white box, and on the lid Gloria’s 5, ringed in grease pencil. “You brought something.”
body.else: Mémère sees it from the head of the table: the white box, and purple coming through at one corner of the cardboard. “You brought something.”

body: “It’s from a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years, ma’am,” Jack says, over the baby. “She says you don’t walk into somebody’s house empty-handed.”
Mémère holds her hand out without taking her eyes off him. Celeste puts a fork in it, and cuts a sliver from the edge of the pie with a butter knife, and passes it up the table on a paper towel.

body.text: Mémère eats it slowly. “*Bon.*” She gives the fork back to Celeste and says to her, in French, not low: “*Il a pas écouté.*” And Celeste looks down the table at Jack, and doesn’t quite manage to hide it.
body.else: Mémère eats it slowly. “*Ça tache.*” She finishes it anyway. “*Bon.*”

body: Julian’s box comes next. Celeste brings it out of the house and sets it at her own place and unties the twine both ways with quick competent fingers, and folds back the brown paper. Inside, on a bed of tissue, is a CD in a sleeve lettered by hand, FOR LUCILLE, and under it, smaller, *songs for going to sleep*; and an envelope in the same careful upright hand, to Mrs. Broussard. Celeste reads the card to herself. She holds up the CD and turns it round so the table can see.
“*Le petit violon*,” Mémère says, approving.
“That boy,” says Celeste, and puts the card in her cardigan pocket.
Tony takes the CD from her and turns it over and reads the back, and shakes his head over it in admiration. “Now *that’s* a son-in-law.”

The CD goes from hand to hand down the newspaper, and everybody has a good word for it, and Jack sits in the chair Celeste put him in with Lucille asleep against his arm, and not one person at the table finds anything to correct. He takes a crawfish off the pile with his free hand and tries to peel it one-handed. It comes apart in three pieces, and something hot squirts him in the eye.
“You’re doing it wrong,” Josie tells him, from across the table.

A quarter of an hour in, the screen door bangs and Lena comes down the back steps into the light in a purple LSU sweatshirt that has to be Remy’s, the sleeves down over her hands, sleep on her face and her hair flat on one side and loose on the other. Lucille has started to fuss, and Jack is on his feet handing her back across the table to Tess when Remy slides into his chair behind him.
“Thank you, brother-in-law.”

Lena drops onto the end of the bench beside it. And without looking, she reaches back and takes a fistful of the back of his shirt and pulls him down onto the bench next to her, as if it were always his seat.
The table registers it, and keeps eating. Across the shells Theo’s eyes go to Laney, and Laney’s are already on Theo, and both of them find something urgent to do with the corn.
Lena reaches over and takes her pencil out of his shirt pocket, and twists her hair up off her neck, and puts the pencil through it. She looks at what he has done to the crawfish on his paper towel.

“Lord have mercy.” She takes a fresh one off the pile, puts it in his hands and puts her hands over his. Hers are hot from the pile, and slick with it, and quick. “Pinch.” Her thumbs on his thumbs, at the joint where the head meets the tail; there’s a split at the side of his thumbnail, and the cayenne finds it, and so does she. “Twist.” The head comes off. “Now the end of the tail, there. Squeeze. Pull.” The meat slides out in one piece, pink and curled, and she takes her hands back and takes the tail out of his fingers and eats it herself.
While he is doing the next one on his own she steals the potato off his paper towel.

body.text: When Tony comes by with the pitcher she takes the jelly glass out of Jack’s hand, finishes what’s in it, and gives him back the empty. “Daddy makes them for Louisiana,” she tells him.
body.else: Halfway down the pile she takes his Abita from beside his elbow and drinks from it, a long pull, without asking, and puts it back where it was with the label turned the way he had it.

body: Tony leans down the table on his forearms. “Thirty-five hours, cher. In a Honda.”
“We did thirty-five hours,” Lena says, peeling. “Kevin has the clock.”
Jack keeps his eyes on his crawfish. Under the table her knee comes over against his, and it stays.

body.text: The pie box sits open on the newspaper with two slivers gone. Lena looks at the lid, at the 5 ringed in Gloria’s grease pencil, a second longer than a lid needs.

body: There are blue crabs on the paper, boiled orange, and Rosie asked for a report. Jack wipes his fingers on his jeans and gets the RAZR out.

He does.

journal.text: Marionberry: 4/10. Olallieberry: 9/10 — Dad would eat two pieces and complain about the second. Gloria rated Lena: pecan. She rated Margot without meeting her: rhubarb — tart, and nobody can decide if it’s a fruit. She rated Becca without meeting her: apple. Honest crust. Nobody loses sleep over an apple. Then she asked what happened to the pecan. A whole pie for a funeral is half price. I work here Tue/Thu/Sat, seven to one. Once a year the kitchen goes dark on a Thursday. Saturday the 10th Gloria met Becca: ‘Apple. Told you, hon.’ She looked at Wes a long time. ‘Peach.’ Everybody likes a peach, she says. Saturday the 12th: boysenberry, for a girl off the TV. Sweet up front, tart after. It stains. Saturday on Dupre Street Mémère tasted Gloria’s pecan off a fork. *Bon.*

journal.title: Rosie
journal.text: Rosie Costigan, eight. Drew Theo as a prince before she ever met him. Drew him again in Dad’s parka. He kept both. Christmas Eve she said grace — the baby in New Orleans, Danny, Nonna’s hand, Theo’s mom’s coach. Christmas night she drew the TV girl, with me and a crab. Rosie’s midnight is at nine, off a tape Dad made in 1999. Pots and pans on the porch. Asleep by a quarter past with the spoon. Counted her New Year’s lentils out like coins. Put the three kings at the manger on the sixth. Drew me a plane with the crab in the next seat. Saturday from New Orleans, for her list: *Callinectes sapidus*, confirmed. *Procambarus clarkii* — a girl from New Orleans said. Rosie sent the girl her thanks.

s22.slug: SATURDAY · 9:15 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN TABLE — LANDRIEU
body: Celeste sends the two of them inside with the leftover tails and two mixing bowls — “For tomorrow. Peel, don’t eat” — and they end up side by side at the kitchen table, shelling for the game, her elbow knocking his every time she reaches for the bowl and him not moving over, with WWL on the little television on the counter by the bread box and the sound turned up.

It is the kitchen he drew in his head on the phone on Thursday, nearly: the black iron pot on the back burner, the cayenne in its tin beside the stove. He drew fewer saints. There is one on the windowsill, one on the refrigerator with a magnet through his halo, and St. Jude on a calendar from the parish, still turned to January. Tony stands at the head of the table with a dish towel over his shoulder. Luc leans on the counter with his arms crossed. In the doorway from the hall Mémère has set herself up in a kitchen chair with her jelly glass, where she can see the television and the stairs both.

On the screen the numbers come up in a box in the corner, and the two anchors keep saying the same thing in different words: it’s over. Landrieu has it outright, about two votes out of every three, no runoff. They cut to his party, a ballroom of people with signs in their hands and their mouths open, and the noise of it comes out of the little speaker like surf. Back at the desk the anchors say he has carried the city across its lines, Black neighborhoods and white.

“A Landrieu is a Landrieu,” Tony says, happy and loud, and pops the dish towel against the counter. “First white mayor since his daddy, and his daddy left in seventy-eight. This town’s been Black most of my life, and it went for him two to one. Look at that, son. Look at that.”

Jack looks at it. Tony said the first part flat and the rest of it proud, and Jack can’t tell yet how the two halves fit together, in Tony or at the kitchen table on Glenwood Avenue, where he has heard men say *the city* and mean a map. He takes the head off a crawfish and puts the tail in the bowl.
At the counter Luc watches the screen with his arms crossed and says nothing at all.

“I’m glad he won,” Lena says. She has a tail between her fingers and is pointing it at the television. “I am. I’m saying it in this kitchen, Daddy, mark it down.” She peels it. “But the city that voted tonight isn’t the city that was here in 2005. There are a hundred thousand people from this city in somebody’s cousin’s house in Houston who’d have had a say.”
“So they come home,” Jack says. “Make it safe enough to come home to. Fix the police, fix the schools —”
“Come home to *what*, Youngstown? You can’t come home to a slab.”
“Two-thirds is two-thirds. In Ohio that’s a landslide.”
“In Youngstown two-thirds is how many people moved to Charlotte.”
“That’s low.”
“That’s *demographics*.”
It goes fast, and it goes the old way, both of them peeling right through it without missing a tail.
“A mayor can’t pour a floodwall, Youngstown. That’s the Corps. That’s federal.”
“A mayor can make people believe somebody’s pouring one.”
“That’s *performing*.” She says it smiling, down at the bowl.
“That’s *governing*. Half of it’s getting people to believe you.”
“And the schools? Half of them are charters now, and nobody can tell you which half is working.”
“They’re open. In Youngstown they closed them.”
“There’ll be folks out on the neutral ground on Canal tonight, for a *mayor*.” She points a tail at him. “You know what that is in this town? That’s Carnival come early.”

Tony stands over them with the dish towel and eggs them on, “Go ’head, cher,” and then, “Ohio, you going to take that?” At the counter something happens at one corner of Luc’s mouth and is put away again.
From the doorway, Mémère: “Y’all fight like married people.”
Not one of them corrects it fast enough. Lena puts a tail in the bowl. Jack puts a tail in the bowl. On the screen somebody throws confetti.

choices.text: “A city’s the people who come back. He won the people who came back.”
choices.key: At the Broussards’ kitchen table Landrieu won outright. You told Lena a city is the people who come back. She asked about the ones who couldn’t.
response: “And the ones who couldn’t?” Lena says. She is smiling down at the bowl when she says it. He has an answer for that, and she has one for his answer, and it goes round twice more, quicker each time, past the point and out the other side, with no hurry on either side to win it.
Tony, who lost the thread two rounds ago and is loving it anyway, reaches behind him and turns the television up so he can hear the anchors over the two of them.

choices.text: “I’d take anybody who fixes the cops. I don’t care who his father was.”
choices.key: At the Broussards’ kitchen table Landrieu won outright. You said you’d take anybody who fixes the cops. Luc looked at you a long second.
response: Luc looks at him a long second from the counter, and says nothing.

Lena’s eyes go from her brother to Jack and back, and she lets that one go, and takes the argument somewhere else, the schools, the levee board, anywhere. Tony, who missed all of it, is explaining the levee board to the confetti.

choices.text: “You’re right about Houston. I didn’t think about who isn’t here.”
choices.key: At the Broussards’ kitchen table Landrieu won outright. You told Lena she was right about the people who aren’t here to vote.
response: She stops with her mouth open, ready for a fight that isn’t coming.

She shuts it. She peels the next tail and puts it in his bowl instead of hers. “Well, I don’t concede nothing,” Tony announces, and takes up the fight himself, Tony against the Corps of Engineers, the levee board and the city of Houston, with the remote pointed at the screen as his witness.

choices.text: “In Youngstown we elected a congressman who went to prison, and he ran again from prison.”
choices.key: At the Broussards’ kitchen table Landrieu won outright. You told the table about Traficant running for Congress from prison. Tony was delighted.
response: Tony is delighted. He takes the dish towel off his shoulder to be delighted properly. “Your daddy vote for him?”
“Pop says he’s *our* crook.”

Tony laughs until he has to hold the counter, and Lena says Louisiana could field a team of those, and Tony says not in *this* kitchen, and they are off again, the three of them, and on the screen the anchors give up and go to commercial.

s23.slug: SATURDAY · 10:40 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE HALL — SKYE
body: The hall runs down the side of the house from the front room to the kitchen, past every bedroom door, and the Broussards have hung it with themselves end to end. A wedding in seventies lapels. Luc in his academy blues. A man in white rubber boots holding up a redfish as long as his leg. A Saints team picture signed in silver ink gone brown. Six First Communions in matching frames, oldest to youngest, the three girls in the same veil, and the middle girl has a gap in her teeth and her chin up, daring the photographer to try it. Jack stops in front of that one.

Behind him in the kitchen WWL is still on Landrieu, and Tony is still agreeing with it at the top of his voice. In the front room Lucille has woken up and has something to say. Out in the side yard Remy is hosing out the pot and singing to it in French, badly.
The RAZR goes in his back pocket, and he feels it more than hears it. SKYE (MISFIT).
He has it open on the first ring with a finger in his other ear. “Hang on. I can’t hear you. Hang on.”
“— *there*?” comes through, very small, from Canada, under a cheer from the kitchen. “Jack. Are you there?”
“I’m here. Let me find somewhere.”

choices.text: Take it out on the front steps.
Take it up to the attic.

s23a.slug: SATURDAY · 10:42 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE ATTIC
body: The attic stairs go up out of a corner of the front room, past Mémère’s armchair, steep as a ladder, through a hatch and into heat. Everything warm the house has done tonight has risen and is up here under the roof: the boil, the stove, the gumbo, everybody. The box fan in the gable window has two settings and is on the louder one, pulling the street in over the mattresses without making a dent. Remy’s overflow beds lie end to end down the middle of the boards, and the points of the roofing nails come through the deck above them in rows.

Kevin is asleep on the mattress by the hatch, zipped to the chin in his sleeping bag, flat on his back, the rosary from the van’s mirror wound through his fingers on his chest. Theo is on the next one with his eyes shut and his breathing very even. He is asleep, he would like it known.
Jack lies down on the last mattress, under the Tiger poster, with the RAZR at his ear and the nails over his face. “Okay,” he says, low. “I’m in the attic.”
“Why are you whispering? Is it a bit?”
“People are asleep.”
“I can hear a fan. It’s February.”
“It doesn’t turn off. It’s got loud and louder.”
On her end a page turns over, and a bedspread shifts under it. “How long did it take?”
“Thirty-five and change.”
“You told me thirty.”
“Theo told me thirty.”
“Ted would. And how was it?”
Jack looks at the nails. “Long.”
“Long is a running time, Jack,” Skye says. “I asked for a review.”

“Theo had a room at the Roosevelt,” he says. “An eighty-eight-year-old woman in a cardigan cancelled it for him on the porch. She said, You sleep here. He said, Yes, ma’am. So he’s sleeping here. He’s on the next mattress.”
“Is he asleep?”
Jack looks over. Theo’s eyes are shut. “He says so.”
“He has never been asleep in his life when there was something to hear,” Skye says. “Hi, Ted.”
On the next mattress Theo goes on being asleep.
“You were in my single today,” she says.
“Your what?”

“My single. The shot that’s only me. Cassie’s porch, take nine, and there you were, left shoulder, in my single. You held very still. You didn’t pull focus. The director looked at the monitor and said, The shirt’s reading, which is the nicest thing he’s said to anybody all week.”
“Did you tell him whose it was?”
“I told him it was method.” Another page. “I’m on a hotel bed the size of a parking space with tomorrow’s sides on my stomach, and I am not going to look at them. Read me the rude ones. Those first.”
The streetlight comes in around the edges of the fan. He holds the book up into it, pages through to Binx going on about his malaise, and reads her the pencil beside it: *Dyspepsia. Have a gin.*

Skye laughs with all the sound in it, and he turns the phone into the mattress to keep it off the sleepers. “Oh, he’s *awful*. He’s awful and he’s right. That’s every note I’ve ever gotten from a network. Another one.”
He finds Aunt Emily laying down the law to Binx about how a gentleman conducts himself, and beside her: *The old girl is right and I should hate to tell her so.*
That one she takes quietly. “That’s not rude.”
“It’s a little rude.”
“It’s the nicest thing in the book. You can tell he lost an argument to a woman exactly like her once, and never got over it, and never wanted to.”

body.text: “You said you’d call at the kickoff,” Skye says. “I’m holding you to it. I’ll be in a trailer. I’ll be cheering for the wrong people, to keep it interesting.”
body.else: “Tomorrow’s your game,” Skye says. “Call me at the kickoff. I’ll be in a trailer. I’ll be cheering for the wrong people, to keep it interesting.”

body: “Don’t you dare,” he says.
“Quietly,” Skye says. “Into a wig.”
Then she’s quiet, and the line has only the hotel on it, a door down a hall, an elevator going somewhere under her.
“I miss you,” Skye says.

At the hatch a plate comes up out of the dark of the stairs, and then Lena as far as her shoulders, in Remy’s LSU sweatshirt. She sets the plate on the boards at the top of the stairs, a bowl on it with steam coming off, and starts back down. By the time he has his head up off the mattress there’s the plate, and her back going down the ladder.
Jack lies under the nails with the phone against his ear and the fan pulling at his hair.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out. Candlemas she held my candle while I knelt. That night she came up to my room for the first time. She didn’t ask. When she asks again, she says, she wants me to have nowhere to be in the morning. She asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. Wednesday on the swing, coats on, she kept me in the daylight. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks, a pilot, from Friday. She told me to go to New Orleans and watch my Saints win. Maybe it’ll be good for you guys, she said. I said yes. Thursday we skipped the rest of the day for the Point. Sol let her into the darkroom in January, for the project. Thursday night it was full of me — asleep, the back of me on the Point, the two of us on the swing — pictures I didn’t know anybody was taking. She gave me the swing: NOT FOR POSTING. It’s in Hale’s book. She propped the door open on purpose. She asked. She was the one who said no. Her father called her Mary Kate. He left in the dark for a five o’clock call when she was four, kissed her, told her to go back to sleep, and didn’t come back. Everybody she’s ever loved had a call time. When I come back she wants the truth, to her face. I promised. She drove me up the hill at three and waited in the Saab under the bell tower with three suitcases in the back. Friday at a quarter to five she stood with us in the lot while Osei blessed the van, with her eyes shut, and looked at the water on the back of her hand. Bye, Coat check. She went north. We went south. Friday at a truck stop under Picacho Peak she called from Burnaby. Wardrobe took my flannel: Cassie wears it; it got the part. The geese are the size of Labradors. I read her one of Hale’s rude ones at the pump. Saturday night she called again after wrap, and I read her two more, under the Broussards’ roof. She wants a call at the kickoff.

response: “Love you,” he says. “Go to sleep.”

response.text: “You skipped Texas,” Skye says, into what sounds like the pillow. “Louisiana counts double.”
response.else: “Love you,” she says. The plain one, from very close to the phone.

response: “Goodnight, Jack.”
The hinge folds shut. On the next mattress Theo lies on his back with his eyes shut and his hands folded on his stomach, laid out for a viewing. “Costigan,” he says to the rafters.
“What.”
“…Nothing.”

response: “Tell Cassie I want my shirt back in two weeks.”
“Cassie says no,” Skye says, at once. “Cassie says possession is nine-tenths of wardrobe. Goodnight, Jack.”
The hinge folds shut. Theo turns over on the next mattress to face the wall, taking most of the sheet with him. “Costigan,” he says.
“What.”
“…Nothing.”

choices.text: “I’m lying in the attic of a house where everybody talks at once. You’d love it.”
choices.key: Saturday night under the Broussards’ roof Skye called after wrap, and you read her two more of Hale’s margins. You told her she’d love this house, where everybody talks at once.
response: “I’m lying in the attic of a house where everybody talks at once,” he says. “You’d love it.”
“I know I would.” She’s most of the way to sleep already. “Goodnight, Jack.”
The hinge folds shut. On the next mattress Theo has an arm across his eyes, against the streetlight or against something. “Costigan.”
“What.”
“…Nothing.”

s23s.slug: SATURDAY · 10:42 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE FRONT STEPS
body: The porch light is a yellow bulb in a wire cage, and it makes a room out of the top of the steps and leaves the rest of Dupre Street to itself. Cars are parked solid on both sides, a fleur-de-lis on every other bumper. Across the way a black-and-gold flag hangs off a porch rail with no wind to move it. From somewhere across the city, too far off to put a direction on, brass comes in on the damp: a tuba walking, the top of a trumpet over it, a parade still going, or the tail of one.
Jack sits down on the top step with the door shut behind him, and the house goes down to a hum in the boards. “Okay. I’m outside. I’m on some steps.”
“I can hear a band,” Skye says. “Why is there a band? Is it for you?”
“It’s for Saturday. They’ve got a lot of them.”
On her end a page turns over, and a bedspread shifts under it. “How long did it take?”
“Thirty-five and change.”
“You told me thirty.”
“Theo told me thirty.”
“Ted would. And how was it?”
Jack watches a cat cross the street and go under a Buick. “Long.”
“Long is a running time, Jack,” Skye says. “I asked for a review.”
“Theo had a room at the Roosevelt,” he says. “An eighty-eight-year-old woman in a cardigan cancelled it for him on the porch. She said, You sleep here. He said, Yes, ma’am.”
The bedspread goes; she’s sitting up. “Ted said *yes, ma’am*. I have watched that boy talk a maître d’ out of a table he never reserved. Who *is* she? Does she have representation?”
“She has a rosary in her cardigan pocket.”
“Then she doesn’t need any.”
Behind him the screen door opens, and Josie comes out barefoot in a Saints T-shirt that reaches her knees and sits down on the step below his. She looks up at him, and at the phone.
“Who’s that?”
“My girlfriend,” Jack says. “In Canada.”
Josie looks at him a while longer. “Oh.”
She gets up and takes the T-shirt back inside, and the screen door bangs once on its spring.
“Who was *that*?”
“Josie. She’s thirteen. She lives here.”

“*In Canada*,” Skye says. “You made me sound like a girl a boy invents at camp. She’s going to tell everybody at school you have a girlfriend in Canada, and nobody’s going to believe her.” And, louder, for Josie’s benefit: “I’m real, Josie. I have elbows. They’ve had meetings about them.”
“How was the porch?”
“You were in my single today.”
“Your what?”

“My single. The shot that’s only me. Cassie’s porch, take nine, and there you were, left shoulder, in my single.” Her voice drops into the pillow. “You held very still. You didn’t pull focus. The director looked at the monitor and said, The shirt’s reading, which is the nicest thing he’s said to anybody all week. I didn’t tell him whose it was.” Another page. “I’m on a hotel bed the size of a parking space with tomorrow’s sides on my stomach, and I am not going to look at them. Read me the rude ones. Those first.”

The book is in his back pocket, where he’s been sitting on it since Baton Rouge. He tips it to the porch light and pages through to Binx going on about his malaise, and beside it, in the small upright pencil: *Dyspepsia. Have a gin.*

Skye laughs with all the sound in it, into the bedspread, longer than the margin has any right to. “Oh, he’s *awful*. He’s awful and he’s right. That’s every note I’ve ever gotten from a network. Another one.”
He turns pages under the bulb to Aunt Emily laying down the law to Binx about how a gentleman conducts himself, and beside her: *The old girl is right and I should hate to tell her so.*
That one she takes quietly. “That’s not rude.”
“It’s a little rude.”
“It’s the nicest thing in the book. You can tell he lost an argument to a woman exactly like her once, and never got over it, and never wanted to.”

body.text: “You said you’d call at the kickoff,” Skye says. “I’m holding you to it. I’ll be in a trailer. I’ll be cheering for the wrong people, to keep it interesting.”
body.else: “Tomorrow’s your game,” Skye says. “Call me at the kickoff. I’ll be in a trailer. I’ll be cheering for the wrong people, to keep it interesting.”

body: “Don’t you dare,” he says.
“Quietly,” Skye says. “Into a wig.”
Then she’s quiet, and the line has only the hotel on it, a door down a hall, an elevator going somewhere under her.
“I miss you,” Skye says.
Jack puts his head back against the porch post and looks up into the yellow of the bulb.

Behind him the screen door opens again, and this time it doesn’t bang. He turns his head. Lena is on the porch in Remy’s LSU sweatshirt with a plate in both hands, a bowl on it, the steam coming up off the bowl into the light.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out. Candlemas she held my candle while I knelt. That night she came up to my room for the first time. She didn’t ask. When she asks again, she says, she wants me to have nowhere to be in the morning. She asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. Wednesday on the swing, coats on, she kept me in the daylight. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks, a pilot, from Friday. She told me to go to New Orleans and watch my Saints win. Maybe it’ll be good for you guys, she said. I said yes. Thursday we skipped the rest of the day for the Point. Sol let her into the darkroom in January, for the project. Thursday night it was full of me — asleep, the back of me on the Point, the two of us on the swing — pictures I didn’t know anybody was taking. She gave me the swing: NOT FOR POSTING. It’s in Hale’s book. She propped the door open on purpose. She asked. She was the one who said no. Her father called her Mary Kate. He left in the dark for a five o’clock call when she was four, kissed her, told her to go back to sleep, and didn’t come back. Everybody she’s ever loved had a call time. When I come back she wants the truth, to her face. I promised. She drove me up the hill at three and waited in the Saab under the bell tower with three suitcases in the back. Friday at a quarter to five she stood with us in the lot while Osei blessed the van, with her eyes shut, and looked at the water on the back of her hand. Bye, Coat check. She went north. We went south. Friday at a truck stop under Picacho Peak she called from Burnaby. Wardrobe took my flannel: Cassie wears it; it got the part. The geese are the size of Labradors. I read her one of Hale’s rude ones at the pump. Saturday night she called again after wrap, and I read her two more, on the Broussards’ front steps. I told Lena’s little sister who she is. My girlfriend. In Canada. She wants a call at the kickoff.

response.text: “You skipped Texas,” Skye says, into what sounds like the pillow. “Louisiana counts double.”

response: “Goodnight, Jack.”

The hinge folds shut. Lena sets the plate on the porch rail at his shoulder, gumbo over rice with a spoon standing in it and a paper towel folded underneath, and is back inside before he has turned round. When he puts his hands around the bowl it’s still hot.

“Cassie says no,” Skye says, at once. “Cassie says possession is nine-tenths of wardrobe. Goodnight, Jack.”

The hinge folds shut. Lena comes down a step and sets the plate on the step beside him, close enough that the steam comes up past his knee, gumbo over rice with a spoon in it, and is back up the step and through the door without a word.

“I know I would.” She’s most of the way to sleep already. “Goodnight, Jack.”

The hinge folds shut. Behind him Lena crosses the porch and sets the plate on the wide arm of the swing, and the chains creak with it, and the screen door lets her back into the noise. She hasn’t said a word. The plate is gumbo, with the spoon standing up in it.

s24.slug: SATURDAY · 11:40 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE BACK OF THE LOT — THE WATERLINE

body.text: He eats the gumbo on the front steps with the bowl in his lap and the brass coming and going across the city, and when the spoon finds the bottom he takes the bowl back through the house: past Mémère in her armchair in the front room, with the lamp on and her eyes shut; down the hall of First Communions; into a kitchen where Tess is asleep sitting up at the table with Lucille asleep on her, and the TV turned down to a murmur.
body.else: He eats the gumbo sitting on the top step of the attic stairs with his knees up and the fan at his back, and when the spoon finds the bottom he takes the bowl down the ladder and back through the house: past Mémère in her armchair at the foot of it, with the lamp on and her eyes shut; down the hall of First Communions; into a kitchen where Tess is asleep sitting up at the table with Lucille asleep on her, and the TV turned down to a murmur.

body: The sink is stacked to the faucet with the pot’s lid and every bowl the Broussards own. Tony said at the boil that there’s a sink out back by the shed, for the crabs. Jack takes the bowl out the back door and down the steps.

The side yard is dark now. The work light is off, the burner is a black ring on its stand, and the big pot is turned over on the grass to drain. The newspaper has been rolled up around the shells and pushed into a can with the lid set on top at an angle. Out at the back of the lot, by the shed, a small white light is moving on the boards, and it’s Lena’s phone, and Lena, in Remy’s sweatshirt with the sleeves down over her hands, holding it up to the wall.
The yard sink is a concrete tub on a post by the shed door. He runs the tap over the bowl, and the water comes out of it colder than the night.
“Mama’s plate,” she says.
“It was good.”
“It was Mémère’s. Mama just pointed.”
He sets the bowl upside down on the lip of the tub. She brings the light down the boards and holds it still, and he sees what she’s been looking at.

A line runs the length of the shed wall at the height of her shoulder, straight as a chalk line, the brown of strong tea. Somebody has painted the shed white since, two coats by the look of it, and the line has come back up through the paint anyway, a watermark coming up through good paper. Below it the boards are darker, and the grain stands up off them. Above it they’re only old.
“Four and a half feet,” Lena says. “Daddy and his brothers did the house by hand. Two years.”

She doesn’t say anything else. On her the line is at the shoulder. On him it would be across the middle of his chest. Behind them the house is lit in every window and winding down, and out here there’s her light on the boards, and the damp on everything, and her sleeve against his arm, where she leaves it.

choices.text: Put your hand on the line.
choices.key: Out back on Dupre Street Lena showed you the line on the shed where the water stopped. You put your hand on it.
response: He reaches past her and lays his fingers along the line. The boards are cold, and soft with age, and the line under his fingertips is no different from the wood above it or below it. It’s only something you can see.
She watches him do it. She doesn’t say anything. Her thumb finds the button, and the light goes out, and the line goes into the dark with his hand still on it.

choices.text: Ask nothing. Stand with her.
choices.key: Out back on Dupre Street Lena showed you the line on the shed where the water stopped. You asked nothing. You stood there with her.
response: He stands there with her. He looks at the line for as long as she does, with the house loud behind them and her shoulder settling against his arm, and the cold coming up out of the grass into his boots.
When she’s done looking she puts the phone in the front pocket of the sweatshirt, light and all. It glows through the cloth against her stomach, and then that goes too, and the shed is only a shape.

choices.text: “It’s allowed.”
choices.key: Out back on Dupre Street Lena showed you the line on the shed where the water stopped. You said: it’s allowed.
response: “It’s allowed,” he says.

response.text: She turns her face up to him, and he can see she knows where it’s from: the turnout, the guardrail, his father. She looks back at the line, longer this time, with the light steady on it.
response.else: She turns her face up to him and looks at him a long time, out from under the hood of the sweatshirt, with the light still on the boards. Then she looks back at the line.

response: The phone stays in her hand. The screen times out on its own, and the shed goes dark, line and all.

s24a.slug: SATURDAY · 11:50 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE BACK STEPS — TAG
body: When he turns back toward the house there are faces in two windows.

Up under the roof, in the top half of the attic window over the box fan, Theo is looking down at the yard. Below, in the side window of the front room, with the lamp on behind her where Mémère sleeps, Laney is looking down at it too. He sees both of them at once, and then the attic window is only the fan and the front-room window only the lamp.

body.text: His hand is still cold from the boards.
body.else: His hands are in the pockets of the Carhartt.

body: The house is going on without them, quieter now: a television turned low, a spoon in a bowl, the baby stirring and thinking better of it. Lena goes up the back steps ahead of him, and she doesn’t turn around, and she holds the screen door open behind her until his hand is on it.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite.
